articles.title: UAW President Shawn Fain, International Executive Board Sworn In for New Four-Year Term
articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content: United Auto Workers (UAW) President Shawn Fain and the union’s newly elected International Executive Board (IEB) were sworn into office for a new four-year term in a ceremony honoring the will of the membership and reaffirming the union’s commitment to fighting for its members and all working-class people. Press is encouraged to use photos from the swearing-in ceremony . The ceremony marked the beginning of a new term for Fain and the International Executive Board, who pledged to faithfully serve the union’s membership and advance the interests of UAW members, families, and their communities. UAW member and longtime union leader Paul Caucci administered the oath of office to Fain, who begins his second term as International Union president. Fain then administered the constitutional obligation to the newly elected members of the International Executive Board. In remarks following the ceremony, Fain reflected on the responsibility of union leadership and outlined the priorities for the next four years: growing the UAW, building worker power and winning improvements for working-class people. Fain connected the UAW’s history of collective action to the challenges facing workers today, pointing to the legacy of the 1930s sit-down strikes and the union’s more recent Stand Up Strike in 2023. “Our union built the American Dream,” Fain said. “From the Sit Down Strikers of the 1930’s to the Stand-Up Strikers since 2023, regular working-class people have led this union and led this country from the ground up.” “Over the next four years, our job is to do more than just to ensure the survival of our organization,” Fain said. “We need to grow. We need to build. We need to win. And to do that, we need each other.” Fain emphasized that the UAW is a democratic, member-driven organization and that the union’s future depends on members being prepared and empowered to fight for their interests. “This is a democracy,” Fain said. “We are only in this room because the members put us in this room. And we will only win what the members are prepared and empowered to fight for.” The president also highlighted the broader stakes of the labor movement, citing wealth inequality and the influence of corporate power as challenges facing working people. He urged UAW leaders to meet those challenges through faith, solidarity and collective action. “The only path to turning this situation around is by abandoning fear and having faith that’s rooted in solidarity,” Fain said. Fain closed his remarks by calling on the board to approach the next four years with a shared sense of purpose and responsibility. “It’s not our individual legacies on the line. It’s not just our union on the line,” Fain said. “It’s the fate of the working class and the fate of humanity.” “And together, we will rise to the occasion—to meet our generation’s defining moment. And we will do it as a United UAW.” Newly Sworn-In UAW International Executive Board The International Executive Board members sworn into office alongside President Fain are: President: Shawn Fain Secretary-Treasurer: Brandon Campbell Vice President: Laura Dickerson Vice President: Kevin Gotinsky Vice President: Ryan Hiestand Region 1 Director: LaShawn English Region 1A Director: Mark DePaoli Region 1D Director: Scott Zuckschwerdt Region 2B Director: David Green Region 4 Director: Lucas DeSpain Region 6 Director: Mike Miller Region 8 Director: Tim Smith Region 9 Director: Jimmy Lakeman Region 9A Director: Brandon Mancilla The UAW enters its new term focused on expanding the union’s reach through a $100 million investment in new organizing, building worker power and fighting for a better future for workers and their families. As growing wealth inequality threatens the foundations of democracy, the union will confront the challenges and opportunities posed by artificial intelligence and automation, fight for a new trade policy that puts workers first, and fight for a political system that puts workers at the center. The focus of this work will remain the UAW’s core priorities: higher wages, quality health care, retirement security and more time off the job.

articles.title: Economics News for Workers, October 2026
articles.content: On September 16, the Federal Reserve Board raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percent, the first rate hike in three years. Minutes from the meeting which were released in early October indicate that the board of governors expects to impose another rate increase before the end of the year. They meet again on October 28 and December 9. The rate increase, while justified as a means to fight inflation, was primarily meant to reassure international financial markets that the U.S. will make good on its debt, which has spiraled due to the combination of tax cuts for the wealthy and military spending. Higher interest rates are essentially a tax imposed on working people, who will pay higher rates on credit cards and mortgages while also bearing the brunt of slower job growth. (When interest rates are higher, it is more expensive for businesses to borrow money, and they are less likely to expand and hire new workers.) Rising Energy Prices Erase All Wage Gains Since Trump’s Inauguration New data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ September jobs report and Consumer Price Index numbers shows that over the past year, inflation has increased by 3.7 percent, while hourly wage rate increases have fallen to only three percent. This means that the average American worker has seen a 0.7 percent real decline in the value of their wages since September 2025. Or, to put it another way, there has been no net increase in real wages since Trump took office in January, 2025. McDonald’s Using AI to Gouge Consumers In another sign that mature businesses will attempt any tactic to maximize profit, fast food company McDonald’s is now using dynamic pricing based on AI-gathered information. Algorithms track sales across 14,000 restaurants and bring in outside data, such as publicly-posted prices by competitors, to determine how much locals are willing to pay for an item on the menu. A recent article in Reuters notes that comparing two restaurants two miles apart, one is selling a Big Mac for a 21 percent markup over the second. Dynamic pricing has become commonly used by online retailers and rideshare apps like Uber, but the expansion into brick-and-mortar retail is a relatively recent dynamic. Water Bills Up 62 Percent in Last Decade A new study by Food & Water Watch has found that water bills for U.S. households have increased by 62 percent over the past ten years. By comparison, food prices have increased by 30 percent and overall consumer prices by 39 percent in the same period. “Corporate water abuses, federal disinvestment and climate change are supercharging water rate hikes across the country,” said study co-author Mary Grant, the water program director at Food & Water Watch. “Corporate control of water systems exacerbates this affordability crisis, as big water monopolies take away local control, prioritize profit and hike water prices even higher.” The study found that corporate-owner, for-profit water companies charged, on average, 67 percent higher rates than publicly-owned systems. Damaging New Rules on Student Loans Take Effect A new Education Department rule finalized in September means that for the first time, the government will judge eligibility for student loans based upon the “earnings potential” of graduates of the program. Essentially, the department will now look at the average earnings of graduates of a major or degree. If, for example, graduates of a particular bachelor's program make less on average than those with only a high school diploma, the program will be ineligible for federal loans. A defense of the new rule published earlier this year by an American Enterprise Institute fellow who was one of its architects noted the bulk of impacted students were enrolled in “undergraduate certificates” (often at for-profit institutions) in areas like cosmetology and massage therapy, occupations that required no educational background prior to the last few decades of degree inflation. However, the author’s own study also notes that almost two thirds of Master’s degrees in areas like social work and mental health fail to meet the earnings threshold, as the average graduate makes less money than the median worker with just a college degree. Given the pervasive underfunding of social and mental health services, it’s unlikely that the pay scale of these degrees will improve, meaning a critical shortage of new workers in these fields is the most likely outcome. Scammers Rob SNAP Recipients While Trump Administration Does Little to Stop Them Propublica has published an expose on the growing issue of food stamp theft. This is not the theft fearmongered about in right-wing media — recipients using food stamps towards improper purchases — but organized theft of SNAP benefits from recipients . In 2025,this totalled $470 million in benefits, with nearly one million households having had some money stolen. Typically this happens when the mag-stripe information on a card is intercepted (often due to purchases at a disreputable store), with a third party draining the account by purchasing large amounts of baby formula, energy drinks, or other valid SNAP purchase. The thief then resells the purchased product for profit. The most outrageous aspect of this SNAP theft is it would be easy to solve if electronic benefit transfer cards integrated the same sort of chip technology now otherwise universal for credit and debit cards. Indeed, a handful of states, including California, have introduced said cards (which in the case of California, reduced SNAP theft by 83 percent). However, cuts to SNAP funding under the “One Big Beautiful Bill” mean that the vast majority of states are blocked from implementing similar programs. In addition, 2025 cuts made by Elon Musk’s short-lived but highly destructive “Department of Government Oversight” have decimated the number of staff who oversee SNAP. Finally, Trump reversed a Biden-era policy which allowed for recipients to be reimbursed for stolen benefits, meaning that even in the rare cases these scammers are caught, no restitution is paid back to those who had to do without food assistance due to theft.

articles.title: Dattner’s Architects Say They Want a Union
articles.author: Alex N. Press
articles.content: On the west side of Manhattan, near the entrance to the Holland Tunnel, there is a nearly seventy-foot-tall concrete building containing five thousand tons of road salt. The walls of the Spring Street Salt Shed slope inward and outward in enormous pale planes; the whole thing is meant to resemble a grain of salt. Across the street stands a much larger garage that accommodates more than 150 sanitation vehicles, its long facades covered in glass and aluminum louvers. The two buildings were designed together, an attempt to make a sprawling sanitation facility fit into a residential neighborhood where residents had initially fought its construction. Writing about the complex in 2016, Architectural Record called the shed “as compelling as many pieces of public art in Manhattan.” The Salt Shed is a Dattner Architects project, designed with WXY Architecture + Urban Design. So are the 34th Street–Hudson Yards subway station, the Bronx Library Center, parts of Hudson River Park, Riverbank State Park, and thousands of units of housing around New York. Richard Dattner founded the firm in 1964, and public architecture and infrastructure have been central to its work ever since. Now the more than one hundred workers at Dattner are taking an unusual step in their industry: organizing with the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM). The proposed wall-to-wall bargaining unit includes designers, architects, and operations staff across the firm, excluding management and certain other positions. Organizers say they have support from a supermajority of workers. On October 21, Dattner workers will gather at city hall for a listening session with Deputy Mayor Julie Su to discuss the union effort. The meeting comes as workers are pressing the firm’s partners to agree to a process for recognizing their union without a National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) election. “The City has long worked alongside union employers, and we’ve seen the value that worker voice brings to public projects,” said Cassio Mendoza, a spokesperson for Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “We support every worker’s free and fair choice on this question, and the decision belongs to them.” The campaign has been quietly underway for years, extending across Dattner’s three studios and among employees at different points in their careers. Building a supermajority at a firm of this size took time, particularly with workers coming to the campaign for different reasons. “Some might be personal or specific to the firm, while for others, it might be about broader concerns with the industry and previous experiences that they had,” a Dattner designer said. Three Dattner employees spoke to Jacobin for this story. We would ordinarily identify workers discussing their organizing efforts, but there have been allegations of retaliation against union supporters in the architecture industry in recent years. At the firm Snøhetta, eight employees lost their jobs shortly after a 2023 union election. The NLRB later accused the firm of firing them for their union activity. The case has yet to be resolved. We are withholding the Dattner employees’ names so they can speak freely about the campaign. Dattner is, by the accounts of the workers I spoke with, a relatively good place to work. A licensed architect at Dattner described it as a leader in working conditions within the industry. That makes its union campaign an opportunity to set a precedent. “If we don’t lead this effort, if a firm like ours just can’t or won’t lead this effort, who’s going to?” the architect asked. Dattner calls itself a mission-driven firm . Riverbank State Park puts a park atop a wastewater treatment plant; Via Verde, designed with Grimshaw, is a mixed-income housing development in the South Bronx; the 34th Street–Hudson Yards station was the first new subway station to open in the city in more than twenty-five years. Much of the firm’s work is commissioned by public agencies. “We’re trying to create in our work a more democratic city, more democratic spaces for people to live in,” the architect said. “If we want to make more democratic spaces, that starts in the office. And having a more democratic process in the office is only going to allow us to do our jobs better, fulfill our mission better.” The Work Behind the Buildings The architect is easy to imagine somewhere above the city, a kind of deity with the vision to change the landscape of a metropolis and the power to make everyone else go along: scores of people to build it, and the rest of us to live in it. A line on an architectural drawing can eventually become an instruction for many others to build something. But getting from that line to the building requires engineers, contractors, construction workers, clients, and public agencies, along with plenty of work inside the architecture firm itself. The work can mean navigating building codes and zoning rules, responding to clients, and producing and revising digital models and drawings. “There is drudge work,” an associate at Dattner said. “It’s not all drawing pictures and picking colors.” Becoming a licensed architect can take a long time, too. According to the National Council of Architectural Registration Boards, the average person who earned a license in 2025 took 12.3 years to get there, including their education. For all that education and training, architecture is not an especially lucrative profession for many of its practitioners. The profession nevertheless retains a powerful image of the architect as a singular creative genius, a Frank Lloyd Wright whose talent might eventually bring wealth and acclaim. For those who imagine they might someday join his ranks, long hours and modest pay can seem like dues worth paying. “There’s this culture of suffering for the work, of pouring yourself into it because it is this creative discipline,” the Dattner architect said. “I’ve been in situations before where we felt like we needed to explore another idea, we needed to explore another scheme, and it’s just not acceptable to say, ‘We don’t have time for that.’” Long hours are familiar to architects well before they enter the profession. Architecture students routinely spend nights in the studio, and the hours don’t necessarily improve once they’re employed. Firms compete for commissions, often on price, and employees can end up working nights and weekends to get projects finished. “I know many of my classmates who have already left the profession before they got licensed because it wasn’t sustainable for them,” the designer said. The cost of living in New York has made the profession’s pay harder to accept. “My rent costs more money, and I’m more exhausted than I’ve ever been in my life,” the Dattner associate said. “We were all sold this bill of goods: go to college, get educated, become a white-collar professional, and you’re going to have a good life,” said the Dattner architect: We love what we do. I do have a good life, and there are certainly many working-class people who are being squeezed much more. But between the affordability crisis, AI, and discussions of how things need to change in our industry that have been going on for the past decade, it has created a moment where folks like us see an opportunity. People who came before us fought for labor rights, fought for the ability to bargain, and now it’s our time to take up the charge. How Architects Started Organizing Architects have not traditionally thought of themselves as the sort of workers who form unions. But neither did many other white-collar professionals — including graduate students, journalists , and tech workers — who have been organizing in recent years. C. G. Beck, an architect and writer involved in organizing in the industry, welcomed the Dattner campaign. “Dattner’s unionization campaign is a step forward for all workers in our industry,” Beck said. Peggy Deamer, an architect and a founder of the Architecture Lobby , a grassroots organization advocating for better working conditions and unionization in the profession, has spent years urging architects to think of themselves as workers, with the same concerns about pay, hours, and working conditions as anyone else. Through its Architectural Workers United campaign, the IAM has been involved in a small wave of organizing efforts at New York City architecture firms, where private sector unionism had barely existed for generations. In 2021, workers at SHoP Architects filed for an NLRB election with the IAM. They withdrew the petition shortly before the scheduled vote after what the union described as a “powerful anti-union campaign.” In 2022, workers at Bernheimer Architecture took another route: the firm voluntarily recognized its union, the first union at a private sector American architecture firm in decades. The workers ratified a first contract in 2024, winning a thirty-six-hour workweek, compensatory time off for additional hours, and overtime pay after forty-five hours. Workers at Snøhetta voted thirty-five to twenty-nine against unionization in 2023. At Sage and Coombe Architects, workers won voluntary recognition that year and ratified a first contract this spring. Of those campaigns, the two that have reached a first contract were recognized voluntarily. At Dattner, workers have asked management to agree to a process for recognizing the union without an NLRB election. Under the proposed agreement, Dattner would remain neutral while a third party checked whether a majority of employees had signed union cards. The Fight for Recognition On September 23, workers sent Dattner’s partners a letter requesting a card-check neutrality agreement. Six days later, the partners circulated a response to employees, reviewed by Jacobin , calling the IAM’s approach “secretive” and arguing that union representation should be decided through an election, “just as the way we pick a mayor or senator.” Architecture firms have been struggling with a prolonged downturn. According to the American Institute of Architects, firms have reported declining billings for most of the past three and a half years. In August, firms in the Northeast reported their steepest decline since 2020. The partners, meanwhile, warned that unionization could cost Dattner clients, claiming that the small architecture firms where the IAM had won recognition “have not thrived in the wake of unionization and the employees do not seem to have benefitted.” They also claimed that once employees unionized, it would become illegal for management to make individualized accommodations for employees, although federal labor law does not categorically prohibit such arrangements. They further disputed the idea that collective bargaining would give workers a say in which projects the firm pursued or how it conducted business. Dattner’s management did not respond to a request for comment. The organizing committee sent a second letter on October 5. “We are not requesting voluntary recognition, nor an election agreement,” the workers wrote. “Considering the current federal administration, we believe that it would be best for everyone to find a process outside of the NLRB.” They also emphasized that they were not seeking a predetermined union contract. “Our contract is our own,” they wrote. They asked the partners to meet with their union representative and respond by Friday, October 9. In an email to staff on that date, Dattner management wrote that it did not believe card-check neutrality “would be in the best interest of Dattner Architects or our employees.” “Meet us at the table,” the Dattner associate said when asked what she would like to say to Dattner’s management. “We’re ready and excited to talk about the ways that we see this being beneficial, not just for the firm, but for something larger than ourselves.” If the union is recognized, the IAM says, Dattner would become the largest unionized architecture firm in the United States. Workers argued that unionization could help the firm retain employees and appeal to clients that share its commitments. They also hoped to have more influence over how the firm operates, including greater transparency around compensation. “We can’t see the books,” the Dattner associate said. “The office purports to have positive values, including equity, and they tell us that we have pay equity. But we can’t confirm that without really having a seat at the table.” “This is not a movement against anything,” she said. “It is a movement for something. There’s a lot of positive energy among the group about how working as architects doing important work for the city and beyond can be something that also includes a great quality of life and a great working experience.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. Subscribe to the print edition for $20 a year.

articles.title: More Than Ball Fields
articles.author: Bill Gould
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. For generations of Altadena families, Charles S. Farnsworth Park has been much more than ballfields at the foot of the San Gabriel Mountains. It has been one of the places where Altadena comes together. Children learned to throw and catch there, parents watched from the stands, coaches became mentors and neighbors became friends. But Farnsworth has always served a broader community. Its playgrounds, tennis and pickleball courts and basketball courts provided recreation for all ages. The historic Davies Building and amphitheater hosted plays, concerts, voting and community celebrations. Farnsworth was not simply a park; it was part of Altadena’s civic life. As someone whose family lost our home and all of our belongings in the Eaton Fire, I have spent much of the past year thinking and writing about what genuine recovery should mean. I have argued that rebuilding must be centered on people and that survivors should not be left to navigate recovery alone. For many families, this process will take years. That is why rebuilding places like Farnsworth matters. Before the fire, I wrote about my family’s experience with baseball in Altadena. Our son grew up playing with Central Altadena Little League (C.A.L.L.) and the Altadena Baseball Academy, much of it at Farnsworth. I described the park as a “truly picturesque backdrop,” with the San Gabriel Mountains giving Altadena baseball a home-field advantage that had little to do with the scoreboard. Related: Rebuilding After the Eaton Fire: Disaster Recovery Isn’t Working. Here’s What Survivors Really Need The Eaton Fire devastated Altadena in January 2025, destroying thousands of homes and severely damaging Farnsworth. C.A.L.L. suddenly found itself without its longtime home. Yet baseball became one way Altadena refused to surrender its sense of community. That did not happen by accident. C.A.L.L.’s board and league leaders — many of whom lost homes or were displaced — made the remarkable decision to keep the league going. Working with coaches, parents, donors and neighboring leagues that offered fields, they put together a 2025 season and created some normalcy for children experiencing extraordinary disruption. That story became the documentary Going for Home. The Los Angeles Dodgers Foundation’s announcement that it will invest $1.4 million to restore two fields at Farnsworth therefore represents something larger than a sports construction project. Dodgers Dreamfields 69 and 70 will include improved playing surfaces and irrigation, fencing, shade structures, solar-powered scoreboards modeled after those at Dodger Stadium and a STEM Trail incorporating the foundation’s Science of Baseball curriculum. Groundbreaking is scheduled for Nov. 5. For Los Angeles Dodgers Foundation CEO Nichol McKenzie-Whiteman, the devastation gave the organization’s work a different meaning. “The Los Angeles Dodgers Foundation has been revitalizing baseball fields since 2003, but we’ve never had to restore fields due to events like the ones that occurred last year,” McKenzie-Whiteman said. “For me, it put our work in a new light; we’re restoring places that held deep sentimental value for generations of families who gathered and played in these parks.” Norma Garcia, Director of the County of Los Angeles Department of Parks and Recreation, asked the Dodgers Foundation to help with Altadena’s parks. Her department also raised $100,000 from DICK’S Sporting Goods to help pay for stands and shade — important additions for families spending hours at the fields. Garcia said the County has requested FEMA assistance for Farnsworth but, so far, has received no FEMA help for the park. Garcia described the new fields as representing “hope, healing, and renewed opportunities” for Altadena’s young people and families. For Matthew Milton, whose family has deep roots in C.A.L.L., the announcement carries special significance. “This is a blessing,” Milton said. “I’m glad the history of Jackie Robinson from this area has led the Dodgers Foundation to make this meaningful contribution to Altadena.” That connection is fitting. Jackie Robinson’s roots in the Pasadena-Altadena area are an important part of the region’s African American history. C.A.L.L. has also reflected Altadena’s rich African American and Latino history, with generations of players, families and coaches sharing the fields and sustaining youth baseball in the community. The Dreamfields connect that history to another generation of children — perhaps another Jackie Robinson among them — who need places to play, gather and simply be children. C.A.L.L. President Phillip Pollerana said Altadena is excited to get Farnsworth operating again. For Little League families — and a community filled with Dodgers fans — the Dodgers organization’s investment carries practical and symbolic meaning. Dart Cathirell, founder of the Altadena Baseball Academy, is especially pleased the project will include new scoreboards and shaded stands. Cathirell and his coaches have spent years providing young players with instruction, mentorship and opportunities to develop their skills and love of baseball. Those details — scoreboards, shade, fencing and quality playing surfaces — might seem small compared with the enormous challenge of rebuilding Altadena. They are not. Recovery is not simply the reconstruction of houses. Parks, schools, churches, libraries, ballfields and local businesses are connective tissue. They transform a collection of houses into a community. Restoring them gives displaced families another reason to return and gives children back places that defined their lives before the fire. We have already seen that power at Loma Alta Park. Its two Dodgers Dreamfields gave C.A.L.L. a place to play while Farnsworth remained unusable. The 2025 season became extraordinary: Central Altadena’s Braves won the District 17 Tournament of Champions, the first division championship in league history. Altadena’s recovery cannot be measured only by building permits or reconstructed houses. It must also be measured by whether families return, longtime institutions survive, children have safe places to play and neighbors again have places to engage one another.The Dodgers Foundation’s investment cannot solve all of Altadena’s rebuilding challenges. But it demonstrates what meaningful partnership can look like: listening to residents, investing substantial resources and building something intended to endure after the immediate disaster response has faded. Children will run onto the fields at Farnsworth again. Parents will settle into shaded stands. Baseballs will hit gloves, runs will illuminate new scoreboards, and coaches will teach another generation the game. Beyond the ballfields, families will return to Farnsworth’s playgrounds and courts and community life will return to the Davies Building and amphitheater. Against the San Gabriel Mountains, Farnsworth can once again become a place where Altadena gathers. For a community rebuilding from unimaginable loss, we should expect that future, invest in it and work together to make it happen. It will mean a piece of Altadena has returned home.

articles.title: In India, “Cockroaches” Are Leading the Fight for Democracy
articles.author: Prajwal Bhat
articles.content: On October 10, India’s capital city, New Delhi, was turned into a fortress as protesters tried to oppose a countrywide exercise to revise the electoral rolls. The protests were called by the Gen Z movement known as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), working with left-wing student groups, which forced the resignation of the minister of education in July. In response, the Indian government deployed more than twenty thousand police officers and paramilitary personnel, suspended internet access in central Delhi, and barricaded the city center. Thousands of protesters, including the leaders of the CJP and prominent opposition politicians, were detained. The protests stem from a massive government effort, known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), to revise India’s electoral rolls by removing dead, duplicate, and ineligible voters. Concerns intensified in the last month that under the SIR eligible voters are losing their right to vote, with 130 million names left off the draft electoral rolls since the start of the program. The events of the last year are part of a larger pattern that has cast doubts on the legitimacy of India’s elections. There are growing fears the SIR was designed to advance Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s goal of a centralized and authoritarian government. Evidence suggests that it handed Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) an electoral advantage in recent state elections by removing voters from marginalized communities, including Muslim voters. The Gen Z protests have garnered support from a broad spectrum of opposition parties, including those on the Left. But the real energy of the protests is coming from the ingenuity and irreverence of young Indians who have flooded the streets of New Delhi despite the violent crackdown. In a country that has long touted itself as the world’s largest democracy, the developments are striking and could prove a turning point for its future. How Modi Changed India’s Elections While the electoral rolls in India are revised every year to add new voters and remove people who have died or moved away, the SIR, which launched back in June 2025, has inverted the voter registration process for the first time in the country’s history. Instead of election officers verifying voters at their homes, the SIR asked voters to fill out a form and prove their eligibility to vote. Voters are matched against records from a previous SIR conducted between 2002 and 2004 and in many cases asked to provide documents showing they are eligible to vote. Critics of the SIR claim that it is stripping eligible voters from the rolls. The SIR is the work of the Election Commission of India (ECI), the country’s chief electoral body, which oversees national elections and provincial elections, including in states with populations larger than California’s. The commission is led by a three-person panel whose chief, like a Supreme Court judge, can be removed only if the Parliament impeaches them. In a key development in December 2023, the Indian government passed a law making changes to the selection process for choosing election commissioners. The result is that the executive branch of the government now has the most influence in the process. The same law also quietly inserted a clause giving these commissioners legal immunity. Making matters worse, the election commissioner responsible for introducing the SIR, Gyanesh Kumar, just so happens to be the first chief election commissioner appointed under the new law, raising questions about what’s really going on. How Centralization of Voter Rolls Could Thwart Democracy in India Criticism of the SIR intensified after The Indian Express reported on September 23 that two of the three election commissioners were sidelined despite raising objections at least fourteen times about the exercise. Among their criticisms were concerns about the process in which new voters were registered, how names were deleted and restored, who had the power to file appeals against restored voters, and who had access to the voter database. The electoral body has maintained that access to the voters’ list is secure and decentralized, meaning that local electoral officers make the judgment on who stays on the voter list. But the revelations in The Indian Express showed that the SIR was relying on ECINET, a digital platform that logs voters. The result is increasing centralization, giving more control over the voter rolls to the commission’s headquarters in Delhi. In one instance, the newspaper documented that officials in the state of Goa flagged ninety-seven voters who were mistakenly removed. Despite eight emails from Goa’s chief electoral officer to officials in New Delhi, the voters were knocked off the rolls when the deadline passed. India’s principal opposition leader, Rahul Gandhi of the Indian National Congress, alleged that the additions and deletions of voters were undertaken as an exercise to disenfranchise a section of voters critical of Modi’s BJP. In the state of West Bengal, the exercise removed some nine million names from the electoral rolls in the months before the state elections in April 2026. Modi’s BJP won power in the state for the first time in the election. Thirty-four percent of those removed from the rolls were Muslim even though they make up just 27 percent of the state’s population. The BJP has maintained that many Muslims eliminated from the lists were “illegal Bangladeshi migrants,” even though evidence has shown scores of Indian nationals were also removed. Of the few appeals tribunals have decided — under 3 percent of some 2.5 million — about 90 percent ended in restoration. With the BJP falling short of a majority in the 2024 general election, the stakes are high for Modi. The party was forced to form a coalition with regional allies that do not share a Hindu-nationalist ideology. The opposition alliance led by Gandhi’s Congress won 234 seats, thirty-eight seats shy of a majority, despite the Congress having its bank accounts frozen and being comfortably outspent . The result is that for the first time in years many Indians are no longer afraid to openly criticize their government — they are even prepared to fight back. The Rise of India’s Cockroach Movement In May, the curiously named Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) first made global headlines after it hit roughly fifteen million followers on Instagram in a week — then again at the end of July after it forced the resignation of India’s minister of education, no small feat. Though the CJP appeared to come out of nowhere, it was the result of long-simmering tensions in India. It started as a satirical joke made by Abhijeet Dipke, an Indian student in Boston, after India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, likened unemployed young Indians questioning the government to “cockroaches” and “parasites.” Dipke posted a comment on X, “What if all cockroaches came together?” and millions responded. He returned from Boston to New Delhi on June 6 and headed directly to Jantar Mantar, launching a protest against the government’s mishandling of a competitive public exam. Though he had limited experience in political organizing, Dipke joined hands with left-wing student organizations in New Delhi. Their first protest lasted thirty-six days and attracted people from all over India and from all walks of life including a vast number of students, exam aspirants, schoolteachers, construction laborers, activists working with civil society organizations, Dalits, Muslims, and other social minorities. By taking up the issue of competitive exams, the movement’s leaders tapped into frustration among young people in India who have seen pathways to social mobility fall apart in recent years. Among those with graduate and postgraduate degrees, the rate of unemployment is particularly high. More than twelve million candidates applied for 8,868 openings in the state-owned Indian Railways company in 2025. The unemployment crisis is further compounded by the high cost of living, hikes in petrol prices, and the effects of pollution, which has left a near-permanent industrial haze over many Indian cities. The country has touted 7.7 percent growth in GDP numbers for the last fiscal year while ignoring persistent inequities on the ground. A Democracy Under Mortal Threat Despite well-documented inequalities in the country, India has long maintained an orderly and transparent electoral process. But a generation of political observers have now witnessed the erosion of once powerful institutions and the threat of detentions and police action against dissenters. In 2019, as Modi ran for a second term, the Election Commission cleared him in six separate complaints that he had violated the election code of conduct. In his second term, he further undermined the independence of the selection of election commissioners, seen as a fresh attempt to tip the political playing field in favor of his party and turn India into a one-party state. Then in 2024, Modi led an even more divisive campaign even as his opposition decried inaction from the election commission. The SIR exercise too has invited widespread public anger since it asked citizens to submit multiple documents simply to prove their eligibility to vote. In some cases, it even forced people identified as dead to come forward to prove that they were, in fact, alive. On September 24, a day after The Indian Express broke the story on the many inefficiencies of the SIR, Abhijeet Dipke and the Cockroach Janta Party called for a protest seeking the removal of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, and the rollback of the SIR process. And with that, the “cockroaches” kickstarted an even bigger public outcry. Mass Protests Are Needed to Protect Voting Rights As with the summer protests over education reforms, the Gen Z movement hoped to channel the growing anger in India over the undermining of democratic elections. Alongside the Cockroach Janta Party, the left-wing student organization All India Students’ Association (AISA) was credited with some of the more robust protest actions in the past week. AISA is the student wing of the Communist Party of India (Marxist–Leninist) Liberation, and its cadre have had to use all their experience, discipline, and political commitment in organizing mass collective actions in the protests. “[The protests] have opened democracy’s Pandora’s box to talk about all the other ways we can ask for accountability,” said Neha Bora, the president of AISA, speaking to Jacobin before this month’s protests. “The energy from this movement should be put into struggles to build our country anew. . . . We know that every mass protest is the possibility of something new and reinforces the idea there could be an end to this violent period.” The movement’s leaders, including Dipke of the CJP and Bora of AISA, announced a united mass protest on October 10. In response, police in India detained over ten thousand people across the country. Then on the day of the protest, the government deployed the overwhelming force of twenty thousand police and paramilitary personnel in order to prevent protesters from gathering in the city. The unprecedented crackdown has done little to stem the tide, as the opposition parties led by Rahul Gandhi held a protest of their own, marching to the Supreme Court on October 12 along with thousands of people. The sheer number who took to the streets this week was reminiscent of previous mass outcries in the Modi era against the disenfranchisement of India’s Muslim community, and against laws that would have left farmers vulnerable. But those protests faced a similar crackdown from the BJP: smear campaigns against the leaders, the use of excessive police force to stop demonstrations, and the eventual arrest of activists under anti-terror laws. Muslim activists and intellectuals like Sharjeel Imam and Umar Khalid have been jailed without trial for six years. However, the Gen Z movement has posed new questions to the BJP and has made it difficult for the party to control the narrative, despite its influence over mainstream television news channels in India. TV news has tried to paint the protesters as agents of India’s supposed external enemies like Pakistan and China. But the arrest of two of the Cockroach Janta Party’s leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, while they were holding the Indian national flag has made that charge hard to sustain. The movement has not only been able to rapidly form a broad coalition on common social interests; it has also mobilized concerns shared by young Indians across religion, caste, and class divides. It has offered Indians the first real sign of lasting political change — little wonder that Modi is now throwing the full might of the state against them. articles.title: France's Youth Revolt
articles.author: Kevin Anderson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Beginning in the marginalized banlieues, France’s high school revolt has become national in scope, taking on economic and racial oppression as well as police brutality. By October 13, the high school protest movement in France had mushroomed, prompting up to half a million people to take to the streets across the country. On that day, Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg made a solidarity visit to one of the high schools where it all started, Lycée Paul Eluard, in the impoverished Paris banlieue (suburb) of Saint-Denis. Thunberg intoned that “the whole world is watching” and that it is “proud of the French students.” [1] With a two-week school vacation beginning on October 16, it remains to be seen if this remarkable movement, which has already lasted over three weeks, will be able to continue. Nevertheless, a new challenge from the left, and from the youngest of the youth, has been hurled at a racialized capitalist system which in France, as in so many other places, is moving in the direction of outright neofascism. Some three years ago, France experienced another nationwide uprising across its impoverished and ethnically oppressed banlieues and poorer city neighborhoods. On June 27, 2023, police gunned down Nahel Merzouk, a seventeen-year-old of Algerian descent who had refused to stop for questioning. As Nahel lay dead, the banlieues and other marginalized communities exploded, with teens and preteens in the lead. By the time the dust had settled five days later, 250 police stations and outposts had been attacked, 700 police injured, much property had been destroyed, and 3,000 youths had been arrested, many of them to be prosecuted mercilessly and jailed. For the French dominant classes, the mainstream media, the politicians, and the trade union bureaucrats, 2023 was seen as an irrational outburst of little long-term political or social import, something to be swept under the rug and forgotten. Little or nothing was done to address the underlying issues, least of all the country’s rampant police brutality and racial profiling. Related: Beyond Class Struggle: What Marx and Fanon Teach Us About Liberation In some ways, the September–October 2026 youth uprising has been a repeat of 2023. The communities where the current uprising originated are essentially the same as in 2023, and confrontations with the police, or rather vicious police violence against the youth, show that little has changed. The dominant rhetoric among politicians and the corporate media continues to characterize those in revolt as “savages” and the like. But 2026 is more than a larger version of 2023. First, this year’s uprising’s size, scope, and staying power have been greater. In the first week, it spread across high schools in poor and marginalized areas of the Paris region. As it did so, it became no longer only a spontaneous revolt, but also a movement making very concrete demands. Second, it has also spread from the banlieues and poorer city districts to more advantaged, even privileged high schools. It also involved parents, university students, and trade unions. All of this has helped break down the isolation of the banlieues , even if only for a time. Moreover, it has put into action the kinds of social forces that, if acting together, could really uproot the system. Third, partly as a result of these wider solidarities, the movement has been more organized and more political, and has expressed clear and comprehensive demands. This was facilitated by the fact that the uprising was centered in the schools, a more structured venue than an urban community, making its participants, even in the banlieues , less isolated and less vulnerable to demonization as street thugs, “savages,” and so on. Fourth, a greater number of key political figures have openly backed the youth than in 2023. Finally, all this has forced the center-right government to make a few small concessions, even though its main response has been demonization and repression. Because of these wider valences, 2026 is sometimes compared—both in the French media and globally—to the mass student-worker uprisings that were the high-water mark of the revolutionary year 1968, when ten million workers went on strike in the wake of university and workplace occupations. The comparison is surely an exaggeration. Nonetheless, 2026 is indeed a sign of wide and deep unrest of a type that cannot easily be contained by political regimes—like that of the neoliberal Emmanuel Macron in France—that represent a capitalism of austerity and whose support is plummeting. For the two sides of that conjuncture are a surge toward new leftwing political parties like La France Insoumise (LFI), and on the other side, toward the neofascist Rassemblement National (RN). Related: Trump’s “Annihilate Iran” Threat Raises the Specter of Nuclear War How the 2026 revolt unfolded On Friday, September 18, students at Lycée Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, a Paris banlieue , began to demonstrate at their school, soon after their return to classes after the summer break, and following a one-day teachers’ strike. This took place after climate change and massive wildfires had led to an unbearable summer across the country. Students experienced classrooms without air conditioning, in intolerable heat. In addition, classes were too large, school days too long, teachers missing due to lack of replacement hires, and buildings dilapidated. Even toilet paper was sometimes missing. An online student survey carried out by the government amid the ensuing protests found that school days as long as 8:00 am to 6:00 PM were one of the principal complaints, especially given climate change and lack of air conditioning. By the week of September 28, the mobilizations spread across the Paris region and then France as a whole. By Friday, October 2, protests had burst out in over a thousand high schools, with some two hundred being blockaded by students. Violence against property took place in a few locations, with a small fire set at Lycée Rosa Parks in Nantes in northwest France, to take one example. This was seized upon by the center-right government and the far right to brand the students as “savages,” rhetoric in turn used to justify the harsh police response. While the movement began and was most active in the banlieues and poorer urban districts, encompassing both trade schools and academic high schools, it became truly national and multi-class very quickly. For example, students at the prestigious Lycée Henri IV in a wealthy area of Paris—whose alumni include Jean-Paul Sartre, Michel Foucault, and President Macron himself—also went on strike, hanging a banner that read “Solidarity with the high schools.” [2] As journalists for Le Monde observed, “Some mobilized out of necessity, others rather from solidarity.” [3] In a number of extensively reported cases, police brutalized young students, among them a fifteen-year-old boy whose hand was torn off by a police “stun grenade.” This device is severely restricted or banned outright in many other European countries. After two weeks, the police announced that they had detained at least briefly some 6,877 people, 86 percent of them minors. Clearly, the goal of such a wide dragnet was to use fear to discourage participation. [4] Still wider solidarities emerged on October 6, when hundreds of thousands, perhaps even half a million people, took to the streets across France in support of the high schoolers. Some were university students and other older adults, many of whom wore white armbands as a sign that they were there to protect the country’s youth from the police—if necessary, by interposing themselves. Parents and other adults were doing the same outside many high schools. In Saint-Denis, another marginalized Paris suburb, Mayor Bally Bagayoko, a Black activist recently elected as a candidate for LFI, joined student demonstrators in an attempt to shield them from police attack. At universities, including the prestigious Sciences Po in Paris, where Palestine solidarity demonstrations over the past few years have faced surveillance and repression, students also engaged in solidarity actions. After taking over a nearby street, however, Sciences Po students were beaten back by a violent police attack. Related: War, Fascism, and the Revolutionary Roads of the Late Marx Grievances and demands Almost everywhere, students mentioned a multiplicity of issues. In Lille, seventeen-year-old Fanny (who prudently wanted to be quoted only by her first name) singled out “bad conditions in which to study, overcrowded classrooms, and buildings in need of repair.” But Fanny also went deeper, calling out “the climate catastrophe, artificial intelligence that is gobbling up jobs, and the risk that the RN will win the elections,” referring to Marine Le Pen’s neofascist party. [5] On October 8, a declaration from the Coordination Antifasciste also noted the “carceral atmosphere in the high schools.” Others referred to racial and ethnic exclusion and oppression. An in-depth account of the protests in the Paris banlieue of Saint-Denis was published by Christophe Ayad, a journalist who has long distinguished himself by his coverage of both Middle East conflicts and France’s immigrant communities. As Ayad reported, student speakers at an October 4 rally asked, “Why do we have fewer chances than those from Paris?” Others declared, “There is a segregation dividing Paris and the suburbs due to Parcoursup”—a much-criticized online university selection system—“which is totally arbitrary. These inequalities are not normal!” Student speakers also decried media narratives that separated the banlieues from the rest of Paris and demonized banlieue students of color as the source of all violence: “There are the whites on one side, the Blacks and the Arabs on the other,” one said, adding, “When a student is non-white, police violence increases tenfold.” Other student protestors noted anti-Muslim discrimination: “Muslims are treated as enemies.” Still others raised wider, more political slogans, like support for Palestine. While expressing deep alienation, the students also referred to themselves as “the new France,” thus pointing to the more multiethnic and inclusive future society they envision. Mayor Bagayoko received huge applause when he told a crowd, “You honor the Republic; you honor its values; your demands are legitimate.” [6] Everywhere, the slogans reflected the anger, but also the imagination and verve, of a new generation. Referring to the militarized CRS riot police, students chanted, “You were sent an SOS and we received your CRS.” Adopting directly—and in English—a slogan associated with US Black Lives Matter movement, others chanted “ACAB” (All cops are bastards). One handmade sign read “ACAB” and “July 1830,” referring to the revolution that ended Restoration attempts re-establish France’s absolute monarchy. [7] Beyond Class Struggle (36:37) What has been achieved While the specific gains so far are very small, promises to hire three thousand teachers and to suspend layoffs of teachers, this movement’s mere existence and persistence is itself a kind of victory in the face the far-right surge that has been gripping Western Europe, including France. This is particularly significant at a time when both social media and traditional TV and other mass media are increasingly under the control of rightwing oligarchs. The militancy and creativity of the youth have broken through those barriers, just as they have of late in India with the Cockroach Janta Party. The fact that such a militant and large-scale movement took place not in the Global South, but in Western Europe, illustrates the truly international scope of the struggle for human emancipation today. The French high school uprising of 2026 also shows, in a most dramatic manner, that the ballot box is far from the only way to enact social change, or at least to put it on the agenda. Taking to the streets and occupying key institutions is also a model, and a more radical one. Finally, the French youth revolt of 2026 has crossed barriers of race and class that have so often been used by dominant classes, from the days of slavery to today’s racialized capitalism, to keep oppressed sectors apart from each other and from critical intellectuals, thwarting the kind of cross-fertilization that is needed to truly challenge the system. What we have witnessed in France this year is not only an agenda of “unite and fight.” What has emerged is a movement in which the most oppressed sectors of society—youth of color, descendants of immigrants, and children of the working class—have taken the lead. Notes [1] Charlotte Bozonet et al., “Mouvement lycéen,” Le Monde , October 14, 2026. [2] Arthur Carpentier et al., “Le mouvement lycéen s’étend en France,” Le Monde , October 3, 2026. [3] Rémi Ducasse et al., “Nous, on ne veut rien casser, on veut se faire écouter,” Le Monde , October 7, 2026. [ 4] “Lycéens: ce que nous dit le recours massif à la garde vue,” editorial, Le Monde , October 12, 2026) [5] Carpentier et al., “Le mouvement lycéen s’étend en France.” [6] Christophe Ayad, “Dans les quartiers populaires, un mouvement lycéen très politisé, accompagné, mais pas manipulé,” Le Monde , October 7, 2026. [7] Lorraine de Foucher et al., “Les lycéens maintiennent la pression dans la rue,” Le Monde , October 10, 2026. MROnline

articles.title: The Social Reckoning Needed David Fincher
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: Reporting on how badly Aaron Sorkin’s Facebook drama The Social Reckoning is flopping, I won’t bother to do any better than USA Today ’s mild zinger , “Moviegoers are unfriending The Social Reckoning.” Meanwhile, the critically panned horror film Other Mommy is crushing it at the box office. But that’s unsurprising, because The Social Reckoning doesn’t have Jessica Chastain’s grinning, spider-crawling monster-mommy to draw people in during a Halloween season when the horror film pickings this year are rather slim. Of course, as The Social Reckoning ’s featured creature, Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg is pretty monstrous too, but even with Jeremy Strong playing him, he can’t convey the skin-crawling repulsiveness of this deeply weird billionaire tech mogul who strikes the public as so sociopathic, blank-eyed, and uneasy in his own skin that he seems likely to be a member of an alien species colonizing planet Earth. For Sorkin, it’s a very disappointing second bite at the Zuckerberg apple. The Social Network , which Sorkin wrote, had a major impact when it was released in 2010, because David Fincher made use of his remarkable gift for creating a miasma of dread in portraying the steady, willful, self-driven dehumanization of young Mark Zuckerberg. As astutely played by Jesse Eisenberg, Zuckerberg’s inner creep emerges and rapidly takes him over. It’s made aggressive by the competition from legions of other young male creeps around him at Harvard and later in the tech industry. The film gave us a nauseating look at how the most arrogant human scum rose to the top in the unwholesome nerdboy Olympics that gave rise to Silicon Valley and the global tech takeover of all our lives. It’s too bad Fincher wasn’t along for the ride this time. Here, Aaron Sorkin opted to direct his own script, which he’s insisting should not be considered a sequel to the ultra-successful Social Network . That’s a pretty futile stance toward a film that’s inevitably bound to be marketed and regarded as a sequel, especially because Sorkin himself keeps evoking the earlier film. As in The Social Network , for example, The Social Reckoning deploys a complex flashback structure framed by a team of professionals (played by Wunmi Mosaku and Bill Burr among others) serving as Mark Zuckerberg’s legal counsel and trying to coach him into appearing human before he testifies to congress. This involves such tasks as getting Zuckerberg to nod his head, smile, and show a modicum of empathy for anyone in the world, as a regular person might do. It’s a tall order, and Jeremy Strong goes all-out in portraying a man so pathologically icy and stiff that he’s the stuff of either nightmares or farcical comedy. The Sequel That Isn’t a Sequel — or Something Despite Sorkin’s claims that he’s not just made a sequel, he apparently had been fully confident that Jesse Eisenberg, the star of The Social Network , would be returning, noting rather bitterly that “The studio offered him every incentive you can offer an actor to do it.” Eisenberg turned the big-money role down flat, saying he no longer wanted to be identified with Mark Zuckerberg and “was tired or even aggravated by it,” according to Sorkin. Smart. Rising respect for Jesse Eisenberg. Obviously, Aaron Sorkin should never direct an Aaron Sorkin script, because that creates an exponentially greater seismic impact of Sorkin-ness on our quailing human consciousness. The Social Reckoning is a heavy plod of a movie that keeps attempting to weave in lighter qualities, with patented Sorkin rapid-fire dialogue and plenty of comic relief festooning a ponderously serious subject. As in all Sorkin works, like A Few Good Men , The West Wing , and Steve Jobs , the gradual bonding of fractious characters who are temperamentally opposed to each other plays out with maximum corny sentimentality. He undeniably has a good sense as to what works. And yet here, it simply doesn’t. In the end, the film winds up being an overly familiar narrative about real-life whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), who risks the wrath of Zuckerberg by joining forces with Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) to expose what’s dubbed “The Facebook Files,” a series of articles on the deleterious effects of Facebook, Instagram, and other Zuckerberg-dominated internet platforms on an increasingly addicted public. It’s strange how belated a movie this seems, telling us all what we already know as the furious pace of terrible real-life events outruns The Social Reckoning by miles. As Frances, Mikey Madison plays a part completely opposed to her star-making, Oscar-winning portrayal of the vivid, confident, loudmouthed stripper in Sean Baker’s Anora (2024), which is probably one big reason she agreed to do it. As portrayed here, Frances is an introverted and dedicated data scientist who’s bought into the rhetoric about the democratizing ideal of Facebook and is made increasingly uneasy by what she’s finding in practice as a member of the Civic Integrity Team meant to guard the public’s interest. She keeps claiming to love her job at Facebook, but it’s impossible to see what she loves about it, besides the money and being able to eat in fancy restaurants. She works in a friendless hive of grim worker bees where paranoia reigns and no one will even glance at her findings on the dangerous effects of prolonged Facebook use on the public. Mikey Madison — an inherently vibrant performer and compulsively watchable — brings charming humanity and excellent timing to the role, keeping the movie tolerable if not adequate. She lightens up Jeremy Allen White, who’s been sinking into a morass of mockable self-seriousness since his star-making performance in the highly lauded FX series The Bear . He’s not playing one of his brooding depressives here, thank God. Together, Frances and Jeff arrive at the most alarming algorithmic tendency on Facebook, which is driving users toward ever more extreme content, stoking a tendency toward paranoia, self-righteousness, outspoken racism and xenophobia, and knee-jerk outrage that’s already led to the arrest of a former acquaintance of Frances’s. In the film’s opening sequence, we see this acquaintance, an overreactive blonde named Kayleigh (Portia Doubleday), filming her own traffic-stop encounter with the cops, which devolves into her fit of hysteria and ultimate arrest, shrieking racist insults and right-wing talking points as she’s cuffed and carted away. What made a monster of this young woman, whom Frances remembers as a sane and reasonable defender of progressive causes? Well, it’s the same monster-making Facebook practice that the film will present as the main motivating factor behind the violent January 6 attack on the US Capitol by lunatic Donald Trump supporters, many of them members of far-right groups like the Proud Boys and the Oath Keepers, trying to take back the presidency for their addled hero. And that climactic scene is shot here for massive slo-mo impact. Curiously, Sorkin avoids depicting some of the more absurd cosplaying figures, like Jacob Chansley, the “QAnon Shaman” in bison-horn headdress, and Trump entirely. Sorkin apparently wanted to ensure that it stayed a melodramatized American tragedy, uninflected by any element of the darkly ridiculous, that finally shocks even the uber-arrogant Mark Zuckerberg into repentant silence. And yet, of course, it’s ridiculous. A Political Film Hampered by Milquetoast Politics The Social Reckoning ’s politics are quite clear — Sorkin’s usual “progressive” liberal centrism versus the threat of right-wing conservative madness — which makes it a matter of teeth-grinding fury to read that Sorkin denies he has any such intention: I don’t have a political agenda. . . . I am not trying to persuade you of anything. I am trying to captivate you for however long I’ve asked for your attention in a dark theatre. Obviously, [ The Social Reckoning ] is dealing with something serious, but we’re not asking you to eat your vegetables. It’s not Homework: The Movie. We’ve heard this all before. Alejandro González Iñárritu just made the rounds denying any specific political agenda in his new film Digger , which is even more ludicrous in that case. Either the same cowardice seizes directors just as soon as it comes time to promote their films, or they’re getting coached by producers, studio executives, and PR flacks. Or, most likely, both. But Sorkin isn’t fooling anyone. The problem isn’t that the movie is political; it’s that its politics are not up to the task — not even close. Someone eventually will make a great movie about social-media-induced insanity. Unfortunately, The Social Reckoning is far from it, failing even to approach the power of its Fincher-directed (and Sorkin-penned!) predecessor. Maybe, just maybe, the guy who gave us The West Wing just isn’t the man for our times?
