articles.title: Beyond Israeli Apartheid
articles.author: Ramzy Baroud
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Green Party has put the conversation back on track: the problem is not the lack of creative solutions to the Israeli occupation of Palestine. The problem is Zionism itself. To appreciate the significance of Motion A105, adopted by the Green Party of England and Wales on Oct. 4, consider its basic tenets. The party is now formally anti-Zionist. It endorses the Palestinian right of return, supports one democratic state throughout historic Palestine, reaffirms its commitment to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, distinguishes anti-Zionism from antisemitism, and calls for a full arms embargo against Israel. Though the decision may seem revolutionary within British politics, it is hardly revolutionary when examined against the history of Palestinian dispossession, which began long before the Nakba of 1948. Indeed, the Greens are not the first to equate Zionism with racism. That history owes much to Africa’s anticolonial movements and their struggle against apartheid. Ideas once dismissed as radical are increasingly challenging the boundaries of mainstream British politics In 1975, the Organization of African Unity, meeting in Kampala, Uganda, drew explicit parallels between the racial systems governing South Africa, Zimbabwe and occupied Palestine, identifying their common imperialist origins. This position helped lay the groundwork for UN General Assembly Resolution 3379, adopted on Nov. 10, 1975, which determined that Zionism was a form of racism and racial discrimination. Under intense American and Israeli diplomatic pressure , the UN eventually reversed that determination in 1991. Israel, however, was not required to dismantle the discriminatory structures that had prompted the original condemnation. The revocation changed the UN’s position, not the realities confronting Palestinians. Those who yielded to American pressure in 1991 must therefore confront a troubling question of moral responsibility: Did their decision help legitimize the political structures that have sustained Palestinian dispossession, occupation and settler colonialism? The Greens have now reopened that historical debate. But they have also done something more consequential. By adopting the motion with 1,022 votes in favor and 813 against, party members demonstrated that ideas once dismissed as radical are increasingly challenging the boundaries of mainstream British politics. Related: Israel Is Losing Hollywood Yet within this achievement lie important fault lines, revealing the nature of the struggle ahead. Four of the party’s five MPs opposed the resolution. More tellingly, Sandy Ruthven, chair of Amnesty International UK’s charitable trust, resigned his Green Party membership altogether. In explaining his decision, Ruthven accused the party of seeking to court the hard-left vote while failing to confront prejudice within its own ranks. His resignation exposes a contradiction worth examining, particularly given his association with an organization that has already documented Israel’s apartheid against Palestinians. Due to the genocide in Gaza, the Greens have effectively declared that the time for carefully managed criticism has passed. In February 2022, Amnesty International a landmark report concluding that Israel maintained an institutionalized system of oppression and domination over Palestinians that amounted to apartheid. That recognition was belated but critically important. Apartheid, however, does not emerge in an ideological vacuum. It is sustained by political assumptions about belonging, sovereignty, demographic control and the unequal distribution of rights.In February 2022, Amnesty International published a landmark report concluding that Israel maintained an institutionalized system of oppression and domination over Palestinians that amounted to apartheid. That recognition was belated but critically important. Apartheid, however, does not emerge in an ideological vacuum. It is sustained by political assumptions about belonging, sovereignty, demographic control and the unequal distribution of rights. The question, therefore, is not merely whether Israeli apartheid exists but what political principles made its establishment and perpetuation possible. The Zionist movement emerged in late 19th-century Europe as a nationalist project seeking a Jewish homeland, eventually pursuing Jewish statehood in Palestine. Its implementation ultimately led to the mass displacement of Palestinians in 1948. The connection between that foundational project and the discriminatory structures documented by Amnesty is impossible to ignore. How, then, can the likes of Ruthven condemn apartheid without confronting the ideology that underpins it? And if that ideology is not Zionism, what is it? Related: Iran War Exposing Limits of U.S. Power The larger issue, however, is not a lack of historical knowledge among Britain’s political and intellectual elites. Rather, these elites have long positioned themselves as guardians of the permissible discourse on Israel and Palestine — a narrative that accommodates occasional criticism, sometimes even harsh condemnation, but rarely permits a fundamental challenge to the political structures themselves. The Green Party’s grassroots have now challenged that conventional wisdom. They have crossed the boundary separating what may be criticized from what must remain politically untouchable. Due to the ongoing Israeli genocide in Gaza, the Greens have effectively declared that the time for carefully managed criticism has passed. In doing so, they have opened a political space that others may eventually occupy, including the Labour Party, which is divided between its historically progressive grassroots and an increasingly centrist leadership whose policies, particularly on Palestine, have become virtually indistinguishable from those of the political right. The vote could also encourage similar debates across Europe, challenging political parties to confront the relationship between Zionism, antisemitism, Palestinian rights and the future of historic Palestine. But perhaps the Greens’ most consequential contribution is that they have challenged the very premise of the debate. For decades, international diplomacy has focused overwhelmingly on finding solutions while leaving the ideological foundations of the existing political order largely unexamined. The Greens have reversed that approach, essentially declaring that no political solution in Palestine, however idealistic or supposedly pragmatic, can coexist with Zionism. The backlash against the Greens was, of course, expected. But so too is the growing determination of British voters to challenge the boundaries of permissible debate across the political spectrum. This could finally open the way for a serious conversation about how the world can hold Israel accountable. Arab News

articles.title: Leftists Should Learn to Organize Like Evangelicals
articles.author: Eric Blanc
articles.content: If progressives and radicals had all read Rick Warren’s The Purpose Driven Church when it came out in 1995, we’d be far stronger today. It’s the most important book on organizing that most leftists haven’t read. Luckily, it’s not too late to discover it. Warren founded Saddleback Church in suburban Orange County in 1980, starting with a Bible study in his home. Fifteen years later, more than ten thousand people were attending its services each weekend, and Saddleback had planted twenty-six other churches. The Purpose Driven Church was Warren’s attempt to explain how he’d done it, so that other pastors could do the same. It became a founding manual of “seeker-sensitive” Evangelicalism, which designs churches around the people who don’t yet attend one. By 2004, Warren’s book had sold more than a million copies, and it has since been translated into over thirty languages. Evangelical megachurches are among the few American membership institutions to grow during the past half-century of community collapse. Just compare the growth of evangelical megachurch weekly participation since 1970 to the decline in yearly attendance at union meetings. Roughly three decades ago, evangelicals like Warren systematized and scaled up organizing for our atomized era. The Left, by contrast, is still searching for a model. With a few partial exceptions, contemporary American liberals and radicals haven’t yet figured out how to build durable membership organizations capable of recruiting, retaining, and developing large numbers of people, beyond a small core of paid staff or self-selecting activists. We’re good at big moments like marches, viral campaigns, rallies, and the occasional electoral upset. We’re much worse at turning those moments into organizations that last — and grow. Warren’s book is a field manual, born from relentless trial and error, full of specific tips about greeters, parking spots, name tags, surveys, and membership classes. “Like a research and development center, we’ve experimented with all kinds of approaches to reaching, teaching, training, and sending out God’s people,” Warren notes. Of course, there are significant ideological differences between today’s evangelical churches and Left organizations; we face distinct structural challenges to succeed, and our organizations require a higher level of deliberative democracy. But what’s striking about Warren’s book is how familiar the problems he discusses are to our movements — and how useful his solutions are. Good labor and community organizers already use some of the following practices, but none of our organizations in the U.S. bring all of them together, much less as systematically as evangelicals. Those who doubt that we can replicate something like Warren’s systematic model need only look abroad to examples like the Workers’ Party of Belgium , which has leaned on similar methods to build thick organization in our socially thin era. Part 1 looks at what Warren teaches about recruitment. Part 2, which I’ll publish next week, turns to what happens once people are inside the door: how to retain and develop members to build an increasingly robust organizing machine. Here, then, are The Purpose Driven Church ’s top fourteen recruitment lessons for the Left. 1. Build the Belonging That Used to Grow Organically Warren’s starting point was that the old social glue was gone. For generations, churches (like unions and political parties) could count on people showing up out of habit and social pressure, since neighborhood communities were so tightly knit. “Instead, membership is now an act of commitment,” he writes. Organizing in hypersprawled Southern California, Warren saw that Americans had become mobile, lonely, isolated, and easily distracted by screens. “We’re experiencing an epidemic of loneliness in society,” he warns. But rather than simply mourn this, he spotted an opening: “This ‘longing for belonging’ provides the church with a timely opportunity. Positioning the church as an extended family, as ‘a place where you are cared for,’ will strike a sensitive chord in many lonely hearts.” Evangelicals like Warren grasped the organizing consequences of community collapse long before the Left did. Much of the progressive movement and the Left still organize as if community already exists and just needs to be mobilized or represented. In today’s atomized conditions, Warren convincingly explains, belonging has to be built deliberately, by design. 2. Let People Belong Before They Believe Belonging before belief is one of the core strategic insights of the seeker-sensitive evangelical movement. Warren’s approach starts from a fishing metaphor. “If your church is serious about reaching the unchurched, you must be willing to put up with people who have a lot of problems. Fishing is often messy and smelly. Many churches want the fish they catch to be already scaled, gutted, cleaned, and cooked. That is why they never reach anyone.” At Saddleback, newcomers were invited to “Come and see!” and weren’t expected to have their lives in order. “At Saddleback Church we do not expect unbelievers to act like believers until they are.” Warren would “rather have a southern California pagan attend our crowd service in shorts and a Budweiser® T-shirt than stay home or go to the beach.” He writes that he lost count of the unmarried couples who started attending while living together and then asked him to marry them once they converted; one pair had been living together for seventeen years. Nor did Warren care much why people first walked in the door. “It doesn’t matter why people initially come to Jesus, what matters is that they come. He can work on their motives, values, and priorities once they enter his presence.” While seeker-sensitive evangelicals let people belong before they believe, liberals and leftists tend to ask people to believe before they belong. This has major organizational repercussions. Warren sets a low bar at the door and a high bar for membership at the same time. “We expect very little from the seeker who is investigating the claims of Christ . . . . On the other hand, we require a major commitment from those who want to join our church.” Most of our organizations do the reverse. The bar at the door is high: you’re expected to know the right vocabulary and hold the right positions. Yet the bar for engagement is actually quite low: click a button, sign up for an email list, or, at most, pay modest dues. Nothing else is expected of you. 3. Study Your Terrain Warren repeatedly warns readers not to copy him. “To artificially plant a Saddleback clone in a different environment is a formula for failure,” he writes. “Even I wouldn’t do everything we do at Saddleback if I were in another part of the country. You must figure out what works best to reach seekers in your local context.” It’s a method, not a formula. Before holding a single service, Warren spent twelve weeks going door-to-door with five survey questions, starting with “What do you think is the greatest need in this area?” Reflecting on the responses he received to the question “If you were to look for a church to attend, what kind of things would you look for?” he recalls: “This single question taught me more about thinking like an unbeliever than my entire seminary training.” What he heard became Saddleback’s blueprint. Locals said sermons were boring, members were cliquish, churches only wanted their money, and the childcare was bad. So Warren rebuilt his preaching, trained greeters, announced every week that visitors weren’t expected to give money, and published strict childcare guidelines. Organizers know this as a listening campaign. The best unions do it before they pick their fights. But most activist groups decide their positions and messaging first, and only then go looking for an audience. Warren’s rule is blunt: “No book or demographic report can replace actually talking with the people in your community.” Asking questions is not just how you find out more; it’s also one of the best ways to get people to eventually open up to whatever you might have to offer. As Warren puts it, “I’ve learned that most people can’t hear until they’ve first been heard.” 4. Treat Recruitment as a Science Unlike much of the Left, Warren realized that just being “right” would not automatically translate into effective recruitment. Getting people through the door had to be treated like a science, full of experiments, rigorous assessments, and readjustments. Warren is refreshingly honest about how much failed. “The truth is, we’ve tried more things that didn’t work at Saddleback than did. We’ve never been afraid of failure; we just call everything an ‘experiment.’” He jokes that he could write another book called 1000 Ways to NOT Grow a Church . The Purpose Driven Church is mercilessly critical of self-flattering metrics. Warren recalls a Peanuts cartoon in which Charlie Brown is practicing archery. “Instead of aiming at a target, he would shoot an arrow at his fence and then walk over and draw a target around wherever the arrow stuck.” Too many churches, he says, do the same: “We just draw a bull’s-eye around whomever we reach and settle for that.” Nonprofits and left organizations do this constantly. Instead of questioning our priors, we declare success no matter what, based on whoever happened to show up. And we often count activity (doors knocked, emails sent, events held) or political righteousness instead of results. Warren insists on judging growth relative to what’s ambitiously possible: “To be realistic, you need to focus on the percentage of population being reached, not the actual numbers.” Above all, Warren refuses to let being correct serve as an excuse for being ineffective. He mocks congregations that treat their marginality as a badge of honor: “Some churches point to their lack of a crowd as proof that they are biblical, orthodox, or Spirit-filled.” Anyone who has spent time in small activist circles will recognize the type. 5. Win Hearts, Not Just Heads Warren, a Southern Baptist preacher who believes in biblical truth, is emphatic that arguments aren’t what win people over. “More people are won to Christ by feeling God’s presence than by all of our apologetic arguments combined. Few people, if any, are converted to Christ on purely intellectual grounds.” His biggest regret from his church’s early years was not taking this seriously enough. “In the first years of Saddleback, I made the mistake of underestimating the power of music so I minimized the use of music in our services.” Why does it matter so much? “A song can often touch people in a way that a sermon can’t. Music can bypass intellectual barriers and take the message straight to the heart.” True to form, Warren figured out what music to play by asking people. He handed out three-by-five-inch cards at a service and asked everyone to write down the call letters of the radio station they listened to. Saddleback soon stopped singing hymns in its services oriented to newcomers, and within a year attendance took off. The press took to calling it “the flock that likes to rock.” Warren admits the switch cost him hundreds of potential members, but he says it won thousands more. “Too many church services resemble a funeral more than a festival,” he writes. On the Left, too many of our meetings resemble a graduate seminar or a wake. It wasn’t always this way: the labor and civil rights movements sang, socialized, and celebrated. Zohran Mamdani’s campaign and New York City Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) soccer leagues have offered glimpses of that tradition’s revival. The challenge now is to make participatory joy the norm, not the exception. 6. Think Like an Outsider “The problem is, the longer you are a believer, the less you think like an unbeliever.” Warren saw two reasons for this. First, insiders stop spending time with outsiders. “One of the greatest barriers to evangelism is that most believers spend all their time with other Christians. They don’t have any non-believing friends. If you don’t spend any time with unbelievers, you won’t understand what they’re thinking.” Second, they start talking in code. Of such pastors, Warren quips: “Every Sunday they speak in an unknown tongue without being charismatic!” Warren warns against “developing such a close-knit fellowship that newcomers are afraid or unable to break into it.” He adds that “the problem with most small churches is that they are all core and nothing else. The same fifty people come to everything the church does.” Whether in church or on the Left, tight bonds are good; tight bonds that nobody new can penetrate are fatal. It’s easy for insiders to conclude that outsiders just aren’t interested, but what Warren saw in the survey results suggested otherwise. None of the complaints were theological, and he didn’t meet many who said they skipped church because they didn’t believe in God. “Most of the unchurched aren’t atheists: They are misinformed, turned off, or too busy.” His conclusion: “Churches need to stop saying people are closed to the Gospel and start finding out how to communicate on the unbeliever’s wavelength.” All of this translates directly. Progressive and left activists often have few apolitical friends, our rhetoric is thick with jargon, and when our efforts fall flat, we’re tempted to blame external conditions or the people we failed to reach. “They’re just not yet ready for our message,” we tell ourselves. “They’ll come around eventually.” But what if the problem is our less-than-effective organizing? 7. Orient to the Unorganized From day one, Warren focused on what we in the labor movement call organizing the unorganized. In his membership class, Warren told transfers from other churches bluntly that “if all you intend to do is attend services, we’d rather save your seat for someone who is an unbeliever.” Being a member of Saddleback meant you were expected to spread the gospel. Ten days before Saddleback’s first Easter service in 1980, Warren and his tiny group hand-addressed and hand-stamped fifteen thousand invitation letters to local homes. The letter opened: “AT LAST! A new church designed for those who’ve given up on traditional church services!” It didn’t mention Jesus or the Bible, and this didn’t go over well with the faithful: “In fact, all of the critical and angry letters I received in response to this first letter came from Christians who questioned why I had not mentioned Jesus or the Bible.” Some even questioned whether Warren himself was saved. But 205 people showed up for that first service, and eighty-two of them converted over the next ten weeks. Warren’s takeaway: “You have to decide who you want to impress.” Leftists face the same choice, and we usually choose wrong. Progressive organizations and nonprofits spend much of their time building coalitions with other existing organizations, most of which are similarly small and/or staff-heavy. Socialist groups tend to orient toward the small existing milieus of the already radicalized, and we struggle to recruit broadly, in part because we’re so focused on looking over our left shoulder. The overwhelming majority of Americans of all racial backgrounds remain unorganized. We have to decide whether our main concern is recruiting those millions or orienting to the thousands of existing leftists and nonprofits. 8. Love the People You’re Trying to Organize For Warren, the most important ingredient in church growth isn’t a technique at all. “Loving unbelievers the way Jesus did is the most overlooked key to growing a church. Without his passion for the lost, we will be unwilling to make the sacrifices necessary to reach them.” Recalling what new converts told him had drawn them to Saddleback, Warren writes, “I’ve never had anyone say, ‘It was because of the Reformation theology you believe.’ . . . Instead, the most common response was, ‘I felt an incredible spirit of love toward me that drew me in.’” The catch is that it’s easy to love those who already come week after week. “Of course, every congregation thinks their church is loving. That’s because the people who think it is unloving aren’t there!” At Saddleback, love for unbelievers was measured above all in the consistent focus placed on bringing in new people. But it also took the form of small sacrifices made for newcomers. Members stood through packed services so visitors could sit. On cold days in the church’s tent, they offered visitors their coats. Progressives and leftists often profess love for the marginalized and the working class in the abstract. Actual people, however, are another matter. Those who disagree with us too often face condescension or outright contempt. People can feel that from a mile away, just as Warren’s visitors could tell whether a church wanted them. In Warren’s words, “There is no method, no program, and no technology that can make up for a lack of love for unbelievers.” The uncomfortable truth behind many nonprofits and socialist organizations is the one Warren saw in small churches: on some unconscious level, we don’t want a crowd — or at least we don’t want it enough to shake up our routines and assumptions. A tight circle of the already convinced is comfortable, as is being a big fish in a small sea. 9. Make Every Member a Recruiter For Warren, growth ran through members’ own relationships. “The fruit of a believer is another believer,” he writes. Saddleback needed advertising only at the start. “Today, with thousands of members inviting friends to our church, advertising is unnecessary.” Warren offers a simple metric: a church should have at least 25 percent more regular attenders than members. If it doesn’t, “it means almost no one in your church is inviting unbelievers to come with them.” At Saddleback, twice as many people attended as were members. And if members don’t bring friends, that should worry leaders: “If most of our members never invite anyone to come to our church, what are they saying (by their actions) about the quality of what our church offers?” Very few liberal or left groups even track whether their members are bringing anybody in. Warren is just as clear about what doesn’t bring in newcomers: “By making members feel guilty for not inviting friends? No. By putting up a big sign that says ‘Visitors Welcome’? No. By cold-calling on homes in your community? Probably not.” That last line should give us pause. Even a big success like Zohran’s campaign relied mostly on volunteers knocking on the doors of strangers, rather than recruiting their coworkers, neighbors, or fellow congregants. Knocking on strangers’ doors can win an election. It’s a much weaker way to build a deep, lasting organization. 10. Build a Front Door for Newcomers As a kid, Warren would sometimes bring non-Christian friends to his father’s church. Inevitably, that would be the Sunday his dad preached on tithing or a visiting missionary showed slides. Eventually he gave up inviting anyone: “I wouldn’t think of inviting my unchurched friends from the office because the service wouldn’t make any sense to them. The messages are for me, the songs are for me, the prayers are prayed in terms I understand, and even the announcements are for me.” The root problem, Warren explains, is that “in every church there is constant tension between the concepts of ‘service’ and ‘serve-us.’ Most churches end up tipping the scales toward meeting members’ needs because the members pay the bills.” His solution: “Create a service that is intentionally designed for your members to bring their friends to.” Saddleback’s weekend services were built for newcomers, while a separate midweek service fed the committed. He also urges churches to keep their internal business far away from visitors. Many of our organizations don’t have a front door at all. There’s often no regular, in-person gathering designed for visitors, and very little serious onboarding. A newcomer’s first experience is often a digital mass call where they make no human connections or a general meeting run for insiders: committee reports, points of order, or faction fights over resolutions they’ve never heard of. That’s a believers’ service, being used as a seeker service. No wonder that so many never come back — or that so few of our members are inclined to invite their friends, family, and neighbors to join in. 11. Engineer Warmth, Don’t Assume It Warren knew that warmth doesn’t happen by accident: “While some relationships will spontaneously develop, the friendship factor in assimilation is too crucial to leave to chance. You can’t just hope members will make friends in the church. You must encourage it, plan for it, structure for it, and facilitate it.” So Saddleback engineered it. The best parking spots were reserved for visitors, and pastors and staff parked on the dirt. There were four distinct types of welcome ministers: parking attendants, greeters, hosts, and ushers. Greeters wore no badges, so newcomers would feel welcomed by friendly members rather than officials. Warren made flash cards to memorize names and knew everyone in his church by name until the church grew past about three thousand people. My favorite of Warren’s practices is the simplest. “In the early years of Saddleback, the members practiced what we called the ‘three-minute rule.’ We all agreed that for the first three minutes after the service was over, members would talk only to people they’d never met.” And Saddleback measured whether it was working. Every first-time visitor got a postcard asking what they noticed first, liked best, and liked least. Nearly 90 percent said the first thing they noticed was the warmth and friendliness of the people. “That response is not an accident. It is the result of an intentional strategy to express love to visitors in a manner that they can comprehend.” But a warm welcome at a big event is not enough for people to belong. Getting newcomers into small groups of about a dozen people that meet up weekly is what keeps them. At Saddleback, such groups brought members together, usually at someone’s home (and often with good food), to study the Bible, forge friendships, support one another, and work on shared projects. “We tell people, ‘You won’t really feel a part of this church family until you join a small group.’” And it paid off. “Small groups are the most effective way of closing the back door of your church. We never worry about losing people who are connected to a small group.” 12. Offer Good News “A lot of preaching is what I call ‘Ain’t it awful!’ preaching. It just complains about our society and makes judgments about people in general. It is long on diagnosis and short on remedy.” Sound familiar? Warren’s point is that people already know things are bad. “They are looking for solutions, not a scolding.” That’s why, he argues, “What people need today are fewer ‘ought-to’ sermons and more ‘how-to’ sermons.” Much of the Left specializes in “Ain’t it awful!” politics: doom-posting, moralizing, and endless exposés of how terrible things are. Though diagnosis matters, people join organizations that offer hope and a practical path forward. This positive vision also shapes how you motivate members. “Never use guilt or pressure to motivate people for ministry. It’s vision that motivates; guilt and pressure only discourage people.” The same goes for money. Warren notes that “people give to vision, not to need” and concludes that “churches with money problems often actually have a vision problem.” As Warren puts it, “People want to join a church that knows where it’s going.” 13. Repeat Your Most Important Points Routine, repetition, and ritual are how we absorb important truths. Referencing the Book of Nehemiah, Warren coined what he calls the Nehemiah Principle: “Vision and purpose must be restated every twenty-six days to keep the church moving in the right direction.” Saddleback repeated its five purposes everywhere: in every membership class, on banners and brochures, and in songs. They were even etched into the glass of the worship center’s foyer. Warren preached the same “state of the church” sermon every January, updating only the illustrations. “Don’t be afraid to repeat yourself, because nobody gets it the first time. I call repeating things over and over in fresh ways ‘creative redundancy.’” He also invested in catchy phrases like “Every member is a minister,” reasoning that “slogans, maxims, mottoes, and pithy phrases are remembered long after sermons are forgotten.” 14. Build Structures That Last Warren closes his recruitment case with a tale of two preachers. George Whitefield preached over eighteen thousand sermons, once addressed nearly one hundred thousand people near Glasgow, and helped spark the Great Awakening in the 1730s. But “Whitefield often left his converts without any organization so the results of his work were of short duration. Today, very few Christians would recognize George Whitefield’s name.” John Wesley preached to huge crowds too. “But Wesley was also an organizer. He created an organizational structure to fulfill his purpose that far outlasted his lifetime.” That structure is called the Methodist Church. The lesson: “For any renewal to last in a church, there must be a structure to nurture and support it.” The American left has been in its Whitefield era for a generation. Since the giant protests against the Iraq War in 2003, we’ve seen one ephemeral explosion after another: the immigrant rights marches of 2006, Occupy, the Women’s March, the 2020 uprising after George Floyd’s murder. Each drew and inspired millions. Few built or strengthened lasting institutional power. Warren saw where that road leads. “If you don’t have a system and a structure to assimilate and keep the people you reach, they won’t stay with your church. You’ll have as many people going out the back door of your church as are coming in the front door.” The deeper lesson is that recruitment is not a one-way funnel but a cycle: recruit, assimilate, develop, deploy, recruit again. The people who come through the front door have to be absorbed into relationships, developed into committed members, and given meaningful work. Then they become the people bringing in and building the next wave. That’s how to turn growth into self-sustaining growth. And it’s where Part 2 — on developing an organizing machine — begins. articles.title: Sweden’s Left Faces a Political Deadlock
articles.author: Rikard Warlenius
articles.content: After four years of a right-wing government that the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) heavily influenced, the parties that refuse to cooperate with the SD secured a narrow victory in the general election on September 13. However, the winning side consists of four parties that are politically very far apart and have so far been unable to agree on a new government. While the Left Party refuses to support a government in which it does not hold cabinet posts, the neoliberal Center Party refuses to support a government that includes Left Party ministers. Nobody wants a snap election or a repeat of the extremely slow, 134-day process of forming a government that followed the 2018 election. But there is still no solution in sight to this stalemate. Ultimately, Sweden’s dilemma is bigger than the question of which parties receive which portfolios. It is whether the parties that claim to defend democracy against the inroads of right-wing populism can win a positive majority for a different economic policy agenda rather than a negative majority against the SD’s influence. Swedish Lessons? For much of the postwar period, Sweden seemed to offer a reassuring lesson for the rest of Europe: a strong labor movement could turn social conflict into universal security, while the far right remained at the margins. That settlement rested not only on strong social ties but on a universalist welfare state whose erosion has not been a single event. It has been a piecemeal dismantling . The SD emerged from the neo-Nazi milieu around Keep Sweden Swedish ( Bevara Sverige Svenskt ) and rebranded itself to take far-right, xenophobic ideas into the mainstream. The other parties of the Right progressively abandoned the cordon sanitaire around it as the SD’s voter support grew. In the 2018 election, the Right still held firm, and a weak centrist government took office. But in the run-up to the 2022 election, the temptation to capitalize on the right-wing majority to form a government proved too strong. Three out of four center-right parties formed an alliance with SD and took over the reins of government. This was a three-party coalition that the Moderate Party led, in which the SD formally did not participate. However, as the largest party within the alliance, the SD exerted a very strong influence over government policy through the Tidö Agreement, named after the palace where the parties negotiated it. Before the 2026 election, Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson went further, promising SD ministerial posts if his bloc won a majority. In exchange, the post of prime minister would remain with the Moderates, even though they were still polling below the SD. We should measure the far right’s advance in Sweden and elsewhere not only in terms of who holds a particular office but also in terms of who shapes the broad political agenda. By that measure, the SD has been remarkably successful: politicians across the Right now voice views that would have been beyond the pale a decade ago. The SD’s growth and the prospect of its formal entry into government have polarized Swedish politics. The Swedish Social Democratic Party (SAP) and Center Party — the only traditional right-wing party that still refuses to govern with the SD — presented themselves above all as guarantors against the SD entering any government. Yet they offered voters few clear political distinctions from the governing bloc beyond that pledge. The four-party opposition grouping of SAP, the Left Party, the Center Party, and the Green Party won 176 seats against 173 for the parties of the Tidö Agreement. Swedes often call this grouping red-green, despite the Center Party’s liberal and economically right-leaning profile. But the arithmetic has not produced a government. The Center Party campaigned on keeping both the Left and SD out of government, while the Left Party’s congress had committed the party to refusing to support a government in which it did not participate. Neither party has yet moved. The result is a political deadlock: there is a parliamentary majority opposed to SD’s entry into government but no agreement on what should replace the current administration. The January Agreement’s Afterlife There is a history behind this impasse. After the prolonged stalemate in 2018–19, the Social Democrats and the Green Party eventually formed a government with the active support of the Center Party and the Liberals. The January Agreement promised to keep both the far right and the Left away from political influence. However, this agreement depended on the passive support of the Left in parliament. To secure the support of the Center Party and the Liberals, SAP and the Greens accepted a program of liberal economic reforms, such as the weakening of employment protections and tax cuts for high-income earners. One clause in the agreement — coined the “humiliation clause” by politicians and analysts alike — stated explicitly that the Left Party was to have no influence over government policy. The Left Party nevertheless allowed the government to form on this basis, because its leaders believed that the Liberals would otherwise switch sides and form a government with the support of the SD. The supporters of the January Agreement presented it as a firewall against the far right. But a firewall built by moving the house to the right is a curious defense. The Left Party declared that its support had limits: if the government moved to implement the agreement’s provisions toward the elimination of rent controls or weakening of labor law, the Left would bring it down. In the summer of 2021, it did just that. Although the SAP soon formed a new government, the episode left a legacy of deep mistrust between the two parties of the labor movement. An SAP-led government, with passive support from the Left, nevertheless presided over tax cuts for high earners and the weakening of the right to strike. Critics warned that, while this arrangement may have temporarily prevented an SD government, in the long term it would be more likely to strengthen the far right. In the end, the January Agreement collapsed, but its governing logic survived. This is a case of technocratic centrism at its worst, where there are few substantial differences between the proposed governing alternatives, and the parties largely ask voters to choose the more popular prime minister. It is also the logic of triangulation. According to this logic, erstwhile left-wing forces should concede the economic terms that the center demands, borrow the language of the Right, and hope that competence can compensate for the absence of a distinctive social project. SD remained outside the cabinet, but the party system increasingly organized itself around its priorities: migration, crime, national identity, and the supposed impossibility of a more generous welfare settlement. The Left Party has spent more than a century outside the national government since its origins as the Communist Party of Sweden in 1921. In that time, it has often supported SAP administrations, because the alternative appeared worse — though in recent times, it has increasingly felt as if the lesser of two evils was only slightly lesser. After the humiliation of the January Agreement, which did not stop SD from heavily influencing the next government, the Left Party’s congress this time decided that the party would not hand its seats to a government it did not join. By making that a congress decision, the party leadership sought to bind itself against the predictable pressure to back down in the name of preventing a right-wing government. The party leadership and its supporters argue that this is a necessary break with a pattern in which the Left supplies votes while the Center Party shapes economic policy. They also argue that ministerial posts are the best way to guarantee influence over the government’s day-to-day decisions. Others in the party suggest that the substance of policy is more important than ministerial posts, and that it may even be an advantage for a fringe party to exert influence without having to take responsibility for all government decisions. Overall, support for the prevailing line remains strong within the party. SAP’s wider political ecosystem is pressing the Left to accept a policy agreement without insisting on entry to government. The left wing of SAP, for example Daniel Suhonen of the think tank Katalys , argues that since the SD grew under a similar arrangement, the Left could do the same. But the comparison misses a crucial difference: the SD benefited from a continental tide of right-wing populism, and parties across the Right were normalizing its political project. Repeating the argument that the Left must always accept less to keep SD out of power will not solve its dilemma. It might also turn out that the SD’s tactics delivered a Pyrrhic victory, at least in terms of voter support. The party saw its support decline for the first time in a general election, finishing at 17.5 percent — significantly lower than the Moderates, who thus regained their position as the largest right-wing party. The Sweden Democrats appear to have suffered a loss of support from both ends. Some voters returned to the center-right parties, presumably satisfied with the SD-inspired tightening of migration policy that the Tidö government implemented. At the same time, the most radical supporters felt that the SD had become far too willing to compromise and opted for smaller parties even further to the right. A Left Under Pressure Despite achieving a respectable 8.4 percent of the vote this time, the Left Party has its own unresolved crisis. The current leadership comes from a close circle of colleagues whose ties go back to the party’s youth organization. For more than a decade, their project has been to show that the party has put its unruly radical past behind it, and that the Left is ready to govern alongside SAP as a junior partner only slightly to its left. Internal critics argue that this drive to make the party both easier for its leadership to control and fit for government has repeatedly undermined its support for traditional left-wing positions. Long-standing members have left amid disputes over the Left Party’s support for arms to Ukraine, its acceptance of the arms race and an expanded military budget, its softened opposition to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and its retreat from a more assertive form of internationalist solidarity. The party’s relationship with the Palestine solidarity movement has become an especially visible flash point. Members have criticized its failure to take a stronger stance on Palestine as well as the absence of the party leadership from weekly demonstrations. These disputes have also sharpened tensions over how the party handles questions of internal dissent, discipline, and public protest. As the election approached, media scrutiny focused on Left candidates — often low on the lists in smaller municipalities — over statements they had made about Israel and Palestine. The cases ranged from explicitly antisemitic remarks to statements supporting armed resistance by Palestinians. The party responded with repeated expulsions. In the heat of the campaign, many activists felt that the party was distancing itself from the Palestine solidarity movement rather than standing with it. Similar conflicts have arisen around other issues. At times they have led well-known members, and some members of parliament, to break away and form new parties or organizations. These breakaways explicitly claim that their new ventures will be more attuned to the demands of social movements. These are recent examples of an age-old tension within the socialist movement: Can a parliamentary party remain rooted in social movements without trying to domesticate them? Despite these incidents, which often involved members with an immigrant background, the party achieved remarkable success precisely in those stigmatized suburbs where first- and second-generation immigrants are most concentrated. Voter turnout is usually low in these districts, and the people who do vote most often support the SAP. But turnout rose this year, and the Left made significant inroads. In many such places, the Left became the largest party. If we put its supporters together with the still substantial number of votes for the Social Democratic Party, the two “red” parties often accounted for over 90 percent of the vote. Statistics from exit polls show that the difference in voting behavior has widened even further. If only “ethnic Swedes” had voted, the Tidö parties would have won, and the same would have been true if only men had voted. Rural areas are now right-wing, while the major cities have a red-green majority. Those who self-identify as workers voted in equal measure for the red-green parties and the Tidö parties. The SAP remains the largest workers’ party with 31 percent, but the SD is the second largest with 25 percent, while the Left has 10 percent. The fact that so many people from migrant backgrounds voted for the Left fueled menacing postelection debates in which both Sweden Democrats and some Moderates claimed that migrants in general and Muslims in particular had decided the election. They often combined this with insinuations of electoral fraud. But it should come as no surprise that this section of the population now votes for the opposition. For the past four years, the government parties have constantly singled it out as problematic and made successive attempts at weakening or even revoking residence permits for recent migrants and their families. The Arithmetic of Exclusion The parliamentary deadlock reflects the existence of two different majorities. There are enough seats to keep SD out of a government, yet on economic questions, a cross-party majority often leans to the right. The Center Party’s red lines on taxation, welfare profits, and public investment would pull any government dependent on it in that direction. The anti-SD majority is therefore a negative one: it can block one outcome without agreeing on a positive program. The Left’s choice is not simply whether to demand ministerial posts. It is whether to accept a policy agreement that leaves it outside government, with the Center Party setting much of the economic direction, or to insist that the party’s voters should also have a share in executive responsibility. The stakes are material as well as symbolic. Without ministers and a role in setting priorities, the Left could again find itself endorsing compromises whose costs fall on its own program and electorate. But holding firm also carries risks: critics may blame the party if the parties cannot form a government, resulting in an early election and possibly the return of the Right. There are two familiar ways to describe this dispute. One is that the Left Party must be responsible and accept a lesser role to keep the SD out. The other is that the Center Party must be responsible and accept the Left Party in government, because the parliamentary numbers require it. Both framings moralize what is fundamentally a political conflict over who gets to govern and whose program counts as reasonable. The conflict has already produced an extraordinary opening scene. The Left Party voted with the Moderates to reelect the Moderate Andreas Norlén as speaker of the parliament. SAP leader Magdalena Andersson then returned her first exploratory mandate, saying she could not form a government under the new parliamentary conditions. On October 2, the speaker gave her a fresh mandate which expired yesterday, October 15, when the SAP proposed a vote on a prime minister and a government consisting only of their own party. It did not pass, since no agreement between the four parties was reached. (Both the Greens and the Left had already stated that they would vote no in this round.) The speaker will now likely pass the exploratory mandate on to the leader of the Moderates, Ulf Kristersson — the recently resigned prime minister — who will have one or two weeks to attempt to form a government. That too will likely end in a vote in which the candidate does not secure a majority, and the ball will once again be in the court of SAP, the Left, the Greens, and the Center Party. After four unsuccessful attempts to elect a prime minister, the law requires that a general election be held. That prospect gives every party a reason to hold its line — and a reason to blame someone else if negotiations collapse. The Center Party’s refusal to govern with the Left also leaves open a dangerous escape route. If talks fail, the Center Party could face pressure to tolerate a center-right government dependent on SD’s support, or even to join a right-wing majority, while SD remains outside the cabinet. The party leaders have explicitly said they will not support a government that relies on SD votes, even if SD receives no ministerial posts. But there may be a clear incentive, in a crisis, for the party to redefine what it means by “reliance.” The Center Cannot Hold by Imitation For SAP, the deeper problem is older. For years it has tried to neutralize the challenge from the Moderate Party by imitating its approach to government. This has meant favoring fiscal caution over public investment and market discipline over democratic control, combined with punitive responses to social insecurity and increasingly restrictive language on migration. That strategy has not defeated the Right. It has merely helped legitimize the discourse of the Right while leaving the Left with fewer convincing answers of its own. It has also led to the worst electoral result for the SAP since the advent of universal suffrage. The same dilemma faces social democracy across Europe. Centrist parties can win office by promising stability and borrowing the Right’s language, but the strategy gives voters little reason to expect a different future. When the mainstream says no alternative is possible, the far right offers the most dramatic alternative of all. There is no denying that the situation is bleak. Nor are there clear-cut answers about what the Left’s strategy should be, either in the broad sense of a political program or, more narrowly, in terms of parliamentary tactics for the Left. The recent election gave a majority to right-leaning economic policies, although the Center Party opposition to SD cuts across this majority. The parliamentary strategy of the Left Party has resulted in serious internal conflicts. Although its vote share of 8.4 percent is slightly better than usual, it does not represent a major success. At the same time, this has been the general trend for parties of the radical left in Western Europe: even when they have not been losing support, they have not been making major breakthroughs. In the absence of a surge of civil unrest or the emergence of a charismatic figure to lead the Left, it’s not clear how things could have been different. Under prevailing conditions, we face the prospect that governments will continue dismantling Sweden’s welfare institutions — either quickly and aggressively with the Right in charge or at a somewhat slower pace under the Social Democrats and their centrist allies. articles.title: Getting Grounded October – Zoning Final Draft Fails Community Gardens and Urban Farms
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Elizabeth Henderson Revisions of zoning codes happen at long intervals, so this is a chance for Rochester to make changes that will govern the city for at least the next decade. The process has been underway for over four years and seems to overwhelm the staff which has not met any of their deadlines. In their revisions, the zoning writers have responded to some of the requests from the Food Policy Council and Urban Agriculture Working Group, but we have more work to do. The April 2026 Draft turns out to be their final language. Now it is up to City Council which has the power to make amendments or to accept the draft as is. If you want to support community gardening, please attend one of these sessions and speak up or send in written comments! The zoning revisions process bears the title Zoning Alignment Project because the zoning is supposed to align with the City’s Rochester 2034 Comprehensive Plan . The vision for the plan is lovely: ”Rochester is a beautiful, progressive, lively, healthy, and welcoming city. We build from strength – leveraging our assets to grow our population, local business community, and tax base. We celebrate our 200th birthday in 2034 as a resilient and confident community where diverse neighborhoods are engaged and thriving; downtown is the vibrant heart of our region; our unique network of active waterfronts is accessible to all; and innovation, adaptation, and inclusion drive us forward.” – The People of Rochester In the spirit of this vision, the Food Policy Council prefaced our comments with this reflection: “Community gardens in Rochester are not evenly distributed resources, and they are not evenly burdened by regulation. Taproot Collective’s 2024 – 25 Gardening Together Study – a site survey of 109 Rochester community gardens and qualitative interviews with eight urban growers – documents what planning maps confirm: the gardens that serve Rochester’s most disinvested neighborhoods, often operating on city-permitted vacant lots with no permanent infrastructure, are run predominantly by Black and brown residents with the least margin to absorb bureaucratic cost or legal uncertainty. These are the gardens that a $100 beehive permit fee prices out. These are the gardens that a 144 sq ft greenhouse cap renders non-compliant. And these are the gardeners who have historically been taught to use toxic practices – including tire planters – because those were the cheap materials available to them. “This is the equity dimension of the ZAP that these comments address. The Rochester Food Policy Council – itself supported by Rochester 2034 Action UAG-1i – urges the City Planning Commission to read its urban agriculture provisions not only as technical land use code, but as environmental justice policy. Rochester 2034 (p. 311) identifies local food and urban agriculture as both climate mitigation and adaptation strategies. The Community Food Systems Plan grounds Goal 3 explicitly in equity and calls for making it “easier for residents to grow food where they live,” with particular attention to neighborhoods facing structural barriers including historical disinvestment. In order to be an equitable and efficient policy, the ZAP must align with both documents. Here is a guide to commenting based on the FPC comments: Garden Investment Security: Rochester 2034 calls for long-term land security in multiple action items: VNT-3a, VNT-4d, and UAG-2a collectively direct the City to create 5 – 10-year permit/lease arrangements and to include long-term garden use provisions in the ZAP rewrite. The ZAP does not implement these actions. The equity dimension is acute. Annual revocability is not a neutral administrative feature – it is a structural barrier that falls hardest on lower-income gardeners who cannot risk multi-year investment in infrastructure on land that can be taken back at any time. The newly released Rochester Community Food System Plan (CFSP) reinforces this finding, noting that land tenure insecurity “discourages long-term investment and planning from gardeners” and that gardeners in disinvested neighborhoods have explicitly called for relief from “complicated communication and processes, uncertain land tenure, and perceived lack of support” (CFSP p. 109). The ZAP should classify gardens as permitted in all residential neighborhoods. Recommendation: To align with Rochester 2034, the city should adopt zoning that clusters development more densely along transit corridors. The city can then designate vacant lots that are not on these corridors for use as greenspace and gardens. Each quadrant should get some. Half the city’s 5000 vacant lots are city property which it spends $260 a piece each year to keep “clean and green.” The city saves money when residents take over. When the city permits residents to use its lots for gardens, those lots can be divided into two distinct categories and clearly labeled as reserved for future development or reserved for use as gardens, farms or green space. The ZGEIS recognizes the distinction, stating: “This use is intended to support nearby residents, so allowing them in residential districts makes sense. Lots reserved for community gardens, as the principal use, would not meet the vision for development along the mixed-use corridors.” But does not take the further step to confirm the value of gardens as a principal use in residential districts. Limitations on Season Extension: Rochester 2034 (p. 311) identifies local food and urban agriculture as both climate mitigation and adaptation strategies. The Community Food Systems Plan grounds Goal 3 explicitly in equity and calls for making it “easier for residents to grow food where they live,” with particular attention to neighborhoods facing structural barriers including historical disinvestment. In order to be an equitable and efficient policy, the ZAP must align with both documents. Rochester 2034 Action UAG-3c explicitly directs the City to “explore support for installation of high tunnels, hoop houses, and other season-extending production aids on City-owned and private land.” The ZAP – which Article 1.2.B requires to implement Rochester 2034 – instead caps community garden greenhouses at 144 square feet and applies a 50% lot-area ceiling to all tunnel structures, treating temporary row covers identically to semi-permanent high tunnels. With climate change, in the Northeast rains are more frequent and come down much harder. Using high tunnels is a way to protect crops from pounding rain, so gardeners or urban farmers might justifiably want to cover as much as 75% of their land in order to have a crop. The April 2026 draft changed the previous limit of 25% to 50%. That is better, but we can ask for more, especially since gardeners might also want to cover 100% of the garden with row covers for a few nights to protect from frost. Recommendation: • Replace the 144 sq ft cap with a lot-coverage percentage, consistent with every peer city reviewed and with UAG-3c. • Clarify Section 14.1.G application to garden lots without principal structures. • Establish grandfathering for existing non-compliant structures. • Create separate standards for high tunnels (permanent/semi-permanent) and low tunnels/row covers (temporary). • Exempt low tunnels and row covers from area calculations entirely. Excessive Fee for Keeping Bees – Recommendation : • Reduce or waive the $100 fee for community garden and urban farm apiaries, particularly those operated by nonprofits or serving low-income populations. • Retain the Section 14.2.B siting standards as written. • Affirm NYS requirement for beekeepers to register their hives with the New York State Department of Agriculture and Markets (https://agriculture.ny.gov/plant-industry/honey-bee-health). • Collaborate with community partners to deliver beekeeping education as part of the permitting process for community gardens and urban farms. Remove Confusion about Garden Beds, Paths and Weeds: Section 16.2.F – General Landscape Requirement requires all non-structure, non-paved lot area to be landscaped with trees, shrubs, live groundcover, and other plantings. Community garden growing beds, mulched paths, and production areas are functional green infrastructure under Rochester 2034’s own framework (UAG p. 321, Vacant Lands p. 171). The FPC requests explicit clarification that these satisfy Section 16.2.F. The equity dimension: any ambiguity in this provision creates enforcement exposure for gardens that are least likely to have legal counsel to navigate it. Clear, affirmative language is needed. Recommendation: • Add explicit language that growing beds, production areas, mulched paths, and other functional garden features satisfy Section 16.2.F for lots used as community gardens or urban farms. Definition of Weeds Needed, Section 16.2.E.2 – Maintenance: Definition of “Weeds” – Recommendation : • Define “weed” in Article 24 to exclude intentionally cultivated native plants, food crops, cover crops, and ecologically functional vegetation. • Add language to Section 16.2.E.2 clarifying that the standard does not apply to intentional plantings in community gardens serving food production, cultural preservation, pollinator support, or ecological function. Reduce Toxics in Landscaping: The ZAP section on landscaping (Section 16 Landscape ) offers the opportunity to limit the use of toxic herbicides and pesticides in the city. There is extensive research on the environmental injustice that low-income people are exposed to significantly more toxics in their living environment than wealthier people. Lead paint, dust, contamination from incinerators and factories are located deliberately in neighborhoods where residents have fewer resources to defend themselves. Section E, on maintenance states: “All landscaping must be maintained free from disease, pests, weeds, and litter.” This is the place to insert – “without the use of carcinogenic or endocrine-disrupting herbicides or pesticides.” The Monroe County Parks including city parks, and the Monroe County Forestry Plan, already have strict limits on the use of toxics only for invasive species or serious diseases. Zoning could hold all landowners to these good practices. City Council Public Hearings: Each of the Rochester City Council District representatives – Vice President LaShay D. Harris (South), Michael A. Patterson (Northeast), Mary Lupien (East) and Bridget A. Monroe (Northwest) – will host an initial public, district meeting in the coming weeks regarding the ZAP legislation currently before City Council. These meetings will be held in each respective Councilmember’s district, and will offer residents an opportunity to voice their opinion on ZAP. Additional meetings will be scheduled as well. No registration is required to attend any of these hearings regardless of where you live. Specific dates and times for the initial District Meetings are as follows: Council Member Michael Patterson (Northeast District): Sept. 29: Rochester Public Market at 5:30pm Sept. 30: Ibero Community Room Council Member Mary Lupien (East District): Oct. 13: Ryan R-Center at 6:00pm Council Member Bridget Monroe (Northwest District): Sept. 28: Edgerton R-Center at 6:00pm Oct. 7: Roback Community Center at 6:00pm Council Member LaShay Harris (South District): Oct. 5: New Life Fellowship at 6:00pm Oct. 14: Olmstead Lodge in Highland Park at 6:00pm Following these initial District Meetings, City Council will host official public hearings with the Evans Administration on Oct. 21 and 22 from 5:00pm – 8:00pm in City Council Chambers. These hearings will be open to attendance by the public and available on the City Council YouTube Channel for those who cannot attend in person. City residents who are unable to make any of the many public meetings can email Council@CityofRochester.Gov , fax (585) 428-6347 or attend City Council’s regular Speak to Council and Public Hearing session on Nov. 12 at 6:00pm. The work session will be held on Oct. 8 in City Hall Room 208A. For more information on the City Council ZAP process, City residents can call the City Council office at (585) 428-7538 or email Council@CityofRochester.Gov . Save this date: the 2027 Rochester Urban Farming Conference will take place Saturday, March 13 from 9:30am – 4:00pm at East High! articles.title: High School Protests Can Transform France’s Election Campaign
articles.author: Solange Manche
articles.content: Since the outbreak of high school blockades and students protests in French Guiana and Mayotte this September , Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s party, La France Insoumise, has continued to rise in the polls. After a rally in Clermont-Ferrand last Sunday, filling the city’s biggest arena — the third-largest in France — Mélenchon was for the first time projected to make it to the runoff of the 2027 presidential election, in all possible scenarios lining up different candidates. Marine Le Pen, projected to win 35 percent of the vote in the first round, will almost certainly be his opponent in the final showdown for power. As the movement has yet to reach its peak, these figures could still radically change. On Tuesday, 480,000 people protested across France . With over a million people having already taken to streets in a mere three days of strikes, May ’68 has become a recurring reference by the press and protesters alike . As calls for a convergence between the “yellow vests” ( gilets jaunes ) and the student movement multiply, this Saturday will see one of the most impressive social movements in France gain further momentum. The Left is now significantly better organized than in successive recent waves of protest. It is quite possible that Mélenchon could become president next year on the wave of this social movement. In anglophone media, some are quick to sound the alarm about the dangers this involves, revealing their blatant disconnect from the material conditions not only of students but from most working people in France and their disregard for the frustrations with a centralized, top-down political system. Talk of twin “extremes” of right and left is rampant , yet seemingly ignorant of the extreme exercise of power under Emmanuel Macron. The infamous Article 49.3 of the constitution, which allows the government to pass legislation without having to seek the Assemblée Nationale’s approval, has been used a record number of times to push through extremely unpopular budget cuts under Macron, including the pension reforms of 2023 (a decision that has since been suspended). Comparisons are often drawn with Michel Rocard, prime minister under Socialist President François Mitterrand, who still holds the record for invoking the much-contested provision twenty-eight times. The crucial difference, however, is that Rocard never resorted to it amid mass protests. With France Insoumise’s new program due to be published on November 6, it is likely to reassert its proposal to abolish Article 49.3 as part of a broader effort to put an end to what the party calls the country’s “presidential monarchy.” Applied to a party broadly comparable to the vision of Zohran Mamdani, or reminiscent of Jeremy Corbyn’s leadership of the Labour Party, this ill-founded demonization of “extremism” tastes suspiciously of newspeak. For we know that France Insoumise’s campaign will run on tackling inflation, investing in the green transition, and reinvigorating left-behind rural areas . The fear of the far right is understandable. However, seeing it as all-powerful reflects a misreading of the French political landscape and of the waves of social resistance that have emerged over the past decade. In this sense, it is also important to realize that the current protests cannot be understood in isolation from the yellow vests movement. The Left, and especially trade unions, are still living with the guilt of not having sprung into action when the yellow vests’ protests and occupations first erupted in November 2018. Due to the unrecognizable nature of its protesters, some of whom had never been politically active before their involvement in this movement, there was considerable political disdain for the yellow vests, who mainly came from France’s nonurban populations. The Confédération Générale du Travail (CGT) trade union, generally considered to be the furthest to the left, was initially very cautious, referring to the outbreak of protests as an instrumentalization of people’s exasperation, orchestrated by an ill-defined far right . The CGT is now taking steps to avoid repeating the same mistake, calling for a “yellow-vest–inspired” mass mobilization against the rising cost of living this coming Saturday. Likewise, whereas the Left, politicians, intellectuals, and activists largely remained focused on urban centers during the yellow vests movement, France Insoumise now visibly addresses these past shortcomings by giving greater attention to rural France. One strand of France Insoumise’s program specifically addresses France’s left-behind rural areas and recalls the yellow vests’ contribution in revealing the inequalities that divide city and country. This also answers criticism of the party being too focused on the main cities. The countryside has been crippled by reduced access to health care — commonly referred to as France’s “medical desert” — public transportation, education, and an erosion of local stores, businesses, and social isolation. In order to invest in these areas, France Insoumise plans to decentralize decision-making on the regional level by prioritizing local politics, investing in public meeting spaces, and by making the countryside the driving force behind the party’s ecological planning ambitions . This also concerns the overseas territories where the current protests first emerged. In the first round of the 2022 presidential elections, Mélenchon was the top candidate in these territories, which the party also described as left-behind, neglected areas. The second round, however, saw the reversal of what happened in metropolitan France, with Marine Le Pen winning by a landslide over Emmanuel Macron. Given the remarkably high abstention rates among these same populations, France Insoumise should not forget these overseas territories . With the protests having started in French Guiana and Mayotte, the student movement has significant potential to drive up the vote. In this respect, it is crucial for the Left not to remain focused on those already politically closest to it but to stand in solidarity with the social movement overseas. Given Le Pen’s strong polling position, the prospect of her winning in 2027 cannot be ruled out. Yet it should also be recognized that the conditions are now radically different from those of the previous presidential election, where she again came in second place. In 2022, when Mélenchon already came close to reaching the second round, there were no ongoing mass protests coinciding with the presidential campaign. By then, the yellow vests movement had already begun to lose momentum, with participation dwindling rapidly following the mass police violence on May Day 2019, before eventually fizzling out during the pandemic. The arrival of COVID-19 also, perhaps ironically, weakened strikes in the health care sector that had overlapped with the yellow vests movement. Now the ground has shifted. The Left appears to have understood whose voices it needs to listen to: those of the voters who formed the backbone of the yellow vests movement — working-class people living outside major urban centers. After all, young people are already primarily voting on the Left and for Mélenchon , discrediting claims that the far right is dominant among young people. A clear direction is emerging, spearheaded by young people who, like the yellow vests before them, have little reason to feel optimistic about their future. articles.title: Polls in the Hole
articles.author: John Peeler
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Republicans hope—and Democrats Fear—that the recent pattern of polls underestimating Republican (and Trump) support will save them this year. And there are certainly grounds to hope that. In 2016, most polls had Trump losing, but of course, he won. Polls overestimated Hillary Clinton’s support by 3 percent. In 2020, polls overestimated Democratic numbers by 4.7 percent (but they won anyway). In 2024, Democrats were overestimated by 2.9 percent, and of course Trump won a narrow victory (not the landslide he claims). The mid-term bias has been smaller. In 2018, GOP support was overestimated by a mere 0.5 percent; in 2022, Democratic support was overstated by a scarcely larger 0.8 percent. There is thus some basis for the hypothesis of anti-Trump bias, but very little to suggest a major pattern in the midterms. Trump may ask us to pretend he’s on the ballot, but he’s not. The polls this year all show a durable and increasing deficit for both Trump and the GOP, including polls that are consistently more pro-Trump than others (e.g., Rasmussen). Little doubt exists that Trump is the most unpopular President in the history of modern polling (post-World War II). Other low-end Presidents included Truman, Carter and G.W. Bush. Related: Receivership: Agenda for a Democratic Congress We’re talking disapproval ratings of over 60 percent, and approvals of under 40 percent. If we take the mid-term pattern of the Trump Era (2016-2026), poll bias would be 1 percent or less. While some close House or Senate races might be tipped by such a small bias, other local factors could well be more important than poll bias in determining the outcome. It is extremely unlikely that such small poll bias could tip the entire national election. I wouldn’t bet the farm on the Republicans winning this year. Now 2028 is a whole different ballgame. In the Trump Era, pro-Democratic poll bias has been 3 percent, 4.7 percent, and 2.9 percent. But if Trump continues to be more than 20 points underwater in his approval ratings, that would overwhelm even a 4 or 5 percent poll bias. And Trump will still not be on the ballot. Much will depend on who the parties’ candidates are, and the issues they campaign on. Related: Will Trump Take Cuba? There is also a higher level reality these days. After fifty years of concentration of wealth, most people are just having a harder time getting by. More people are working two or more jobs. More people are working and homeless. Career stability is increasingly unknown. The immediate political result we have seen since 2016 is that the party out of power wins the presidency and Congress, but does nothing effective to improve people’s lives. The President’s party the loses the midterms and the next presidential election. The outs come back in, and do nothing effective to make life better. Repeat cycle. The Democrats will vary likely win both houses of Congress this year and the presidency in 2028, It will be up to them to break the cycle—or be broken by it.
